atoms.summary: Detect bullish EMA crossover (fast EMA crosses above slow EMA). Common periods: 9/21 (short-term), 50/200 (long-term). Adjust for crypto's 24/7 markets.

props.formula: ema(window_fast)[t-1] <= ema(window_slow)[t-1] and ema(window_fast)[t] > ema(window_slow)[t]

fired.description: True if bullish crossover detected, False otherwise

atoms.title: ema_crossover
atoms.summary: Detect an EMA crossover signal with configurable direction (bullish or bearish). Uses EMA indicator to calculate window_fast and window_slow EMAs. Returns True when a crossover is detected in the specified direction. Bullish crossover: window_fast EMA crosses above window_slow EMA Bearish crossover: window_fast EMA crosses below window_slow EMA The crossover detection compares the previous and current bars: - Bullish: prev window_fast <= prev window_slow AND current window_fast > current window_slow - Bearish: prev window_fast >= prev window_slow AND current window_fast < current window_slow Common periods: 9/21 (short-term), 50/200 (long-term). Adjust for crypto's 24/7 markets.

props.formula: direction == 'bullish': ema(window_fast)[t-1] <= ema(window_slow)[t-1] and ema(window_fast)[t] > ema(window_slow)[t]; direction == 'bearish': ema(window_fast)[t-1] >= ema(window_slow)[t-1] and ema(window_fast)[t] < ema(window_slow)[t]

fired.description: True if crossover detected in the specified direction, False otherwise

atoms.title: eom_bullish
atoms.summary: Check if Ease of Movement indicates bullish (easy upward movement).

atoms.title: epma_cross_down

atoms.title: epma_cross_up
atoms.summary: Detect a bullish EPMA crossover (fast EPMA crosses above slow EPMA).

props.formula: epma(window_fast)[t-1] <= epma(window_slow)[t-1] and epma(window_fast)[t] > epma(window_slow)[t]

fired.description: True if bullish EPMA crossover detected on the current bar

atoms.title: evening_star_trigger
atoms.summary: Check if an evening star pattern completed on the current bar. Three-candle bearish reversal: bullish candle, small-bodied star, then bearish candle closing below midpoint of first.

props.formula: close[t-2] > open[t-2] and body[t-1] <= range[t-1] * body_threshold and close[t] < open[t] and close[t] < (open[t-2] + close[t-2]) / 2

high.description: highest price traded during the bar

low.description: lowest price traded during the bar

body_threshold.description: Maximum body-to-range ratio for middle candle

fired.description: True if evening star detected on current bar, False otherwise

notes: 1. Large bullish candle
2. Small-bodied candle (star) that gaps up
3. Large bearish candle that closes below midpoint of first candle
props.source_wording: Strong reversal patterns. More significant with gap between star and surrounding candles.

atoms.title: gravestone_doji_trigger
atoms.summary: Check if a gravestone doji is detected on the current bar. A doji with open/close near the low and a long upper shadow. Bearish signal at resistance.

props.formula: range[t] > 0 and body[t] <= range[t] * body_threshold and lower_wick[t] <= range[t] * lower_wick_max and upper_wick[t] > body[t]

high.description: highest price traded during the bar

low.description: lowest price traded during the bar

fired.description: True if gravestone doji detected on current bar, False otherwise

atoms.title: hammer_trigger
atoms.summary: Check if a hammer shape is detected on the current bar. Small body at upper end with long lower wick and minimal upper wick. Bullish reversal after downtrend.

props.formula: body[t] > 0 and lower_wick[t] >= body[t] * wick_ratio and upper_wick[t] <= body[t] * upper_wick_max

high.description: highest price traded during the bar

low.description: lowest price traded during the bar

wick_ratio.description: Minimum lower wick to body ratio

upper_wick_max.description: Maximum upper wick to body ratio

fired.description: True if hammer detected on current bar, False otherwise

props.explanation: Appears after a downtrend Long lower wick shows rejection of lower prices Bullish reversal signal
props.source_wording: Small body at upper end, long lower wick (2x+ body length), little or no upper wick.

chapter_variants.formula:
Lower_Wick >= 2 * Body
Upper_Wick <= Body * 0.1
Body in upper 25% of range

atoms.title: hanging_man_trigger
atoms.summary: Check if a hanging man shape is detected on the current bar. Same shape as hammer (small body, long lower wick) but interpreted as a bearish reversal when appearing after an uptrend. DEPRECATED: identical to `hammer_trigger`. `_hanging_man` calls `_hammer` and renames the output, so the two fire on exactly the same bars -- verified identical across 499 bars. A hanging man IS a hammer; what distinguishes them is the prior trend, which this implementation does not encode. Kept because the name is referenced outside this repository (MangroveOracle's signals_metadata.json, strategy cohort files, experiment outputs). Use `hammer_trigger`.

props.formula: body[t] > 0 and lower_wick[t] >= body[t] * wick_ratio and upper_wick[t] <= body[t] * upper_wick_max -- identical arithmetic to hammer_trigger; the two differ only by the prior trend, which this implementation does not encode

high.description: highest price traded during the bar

low.description: lowest price traded during the bar

wick_ratio.description: Minimum lower wick to body ratio

upper_wick_max.description: Maximum upper wick to body ratio

fired.description: True if hanging man detected on current bar, False otherwise

props.explanation: Appears after an uptrend Same structure as hammer but bearish context Warning of potential top
props.source_wording: Small body at upper end, long lower wick (2x+ body length), little or no upper wick.

chapter_variants.formula:
Lower_Wick >= 2 * Body
Upper_Wick <= Body * 0.1
Body in upper 25% of range

atoms.title: is_above_alma
atoms.summary: Check if the current price is above the Arnaud Legoux Moving Average (ALMA). ALMA is a Gaussian-weighted MA that can be tuned to react faster (offset near 1, lower sigma) or smoother (offset near 0, higher sigma).

atoms.title: is_above_dema

props.formula: close[t] > dema[t]

fired.description: True if close > DEMA, False otherwise

atoms.title: is_above_epma
atoms.summary: Check if the current price is above the End Point Moving Average (EPMA / LSMA). EPMA is the endpoint of a linear regression over the window, projecting the trend to "now" rather than averaging past values.

props.formula: close[t] > epma[t]

fired.description: True if close > EPMA, False otherwise

atoms.title: is_above_hma
atoms.summary: Check if the current price is above the Hull Moving Average (HMA). HMA tracks price with very low lag while remaining smoother than WMA. A common crypto trend filter.

atoms.title: is_above_mama
atoms.summary: Check if the current price is above the MESA Adaptive Moving Average (MAMA). MAMA adapts its smoothing to volatility via a Hilbert transform.

atoms.title: is_above_sma
atoms.summary: Check if the current price is above the Simple Moving Average. Uses SMA indicator to calculate the SMA for the given window and returns True if the most recent close price is strictly greater than the SMA value. Returns False if insufficient data is available. atoms.summary: Check if the current price is above the Smoothed Moving Average (SMMA / Wilder's). SMMA uses Wilder's smoothing (alpha=1/n) rather than EMA's 2/(n+1), producing a slower, more stable trend line. Same family used inside RSI and ATR.

fired.description: True if close > SMMA, False otherwise

atoms.title: is_above_t3

atoms.title: is_above_tema

atoms.title: is_above_trima
atoms.summary: Check if the current price is above the Triangular Moving Average (TRIMA). TRIMA is a double-smoothed SMA that weights the middle of the window more heavily, producing a smoother trend line than SMA.

atoms.title: is_above_vwma

atoms.title: nr7_trigger
atoms.summary: Check if a narrow range day is detected on the current bar. Current bar has the smallest range within the window period. Signals volatility compression and imminent breakout. Default window=7 for NR7; use 4 for NR4.

atoms.title: outside_bar_trigger

atoms.title: piercing_line_trigger
atoms.summary: Check if a piercing line pattern completed on the current bar. Bullish reversal: bearish candle followed by bullish candle opening below prior low (classic) or prior close (relaxed) and closing above midpoint of prior body. DEFAULT IS THE RELAXED FORM, because the classic one cannot fire here. It requires the bar to open below the prior LOW, and a 24/7 market does not gap: measured on 1,294 BTC daily bars, the open is below the prior low ZERO times, so require_gap=True yields 0 fires against 63 for the relaxed form. Set require_gap=True only for a market that actually closes.

props.formula: close[t-1] < open[t-1] and close[t] > open[t] and open[t] < close[t-1] and close[t] > close[t-1] + (open[t-1] - close[t-1]) * min_penetration -- open[t] < low[t-1] instead when require_gap is true, which cannot occur in a 24/7 market

high.description: highest price traded during the bar

low.description: lowest price traded during the bar

require_gap.description: If True, requires open below previous low (classic Nison), which cannot occur in a 24/7 market. If False, requires open below previous close

fired.description: True if piercing line detected on current bar, False otherwise

props.explanation: Second candle: opens below first's low (classic) or below first's close (relaxed), closes above midpoint of first Bullish reversal at support Note: The classic definition requires a gap (open below previous low), which is rare in 24/7 crypto/forex markets. The `require_gap` parameter controls this -- set to `False` for crypto.
props.source_wording: First candle: bearish

atoms.title: shooting_star_trigger
atoms.summary: Check if a shooting star shape is detected on the current bar. Small body at lower end with long upper wick and minimal lower wick. Bearish reversal after uptrend. DEPRECATED: identical to `inverted_hammer_trigger`. `_shooting_star` calls `_inverted_hammer` and renames the output, so the two fire on exactly the same bars -- verified identical across 499 bars. The distinction is the prior trend, which this implementation does not encode. Kept because the name is referenced outside this repository. Use `inverted_hammer_trigger`.

props.formula: body[t] > 0 and upper_wick[t] >= body[t] * wick_ratio and lower_wick[t] <= body[t] * lower_wick_max -- identical arithmetic to inverted_hammer_trigger; the two differ only by the prior trend, which this implementation does not encode

high.description: highest price traded during the bar

low.description: lowest price traded during the bar

wick_ratio.description: Minimum upper wick to body ratio

lower_wick_max.description: Maximum lower wick to body ratio

fired.description: True if shooting star detected on current bar, False otherwise

props.explanation: Appears after an uptrend Long upper wick shows rejection of higher prices Bearish reversal signal
props.source_wording: Small body at lower end, long upper wick (2x+ body length), little or no lower wick.

Upper_Wick >= 2 * Body
Lower_Wick <= Body * 0.1
Body in lower 25% of range

atoms.title: sma_cross_down
atoms.summary: Detect a bearish SMA crossover as an exit signal. Returns True when the window_fast SMA crosses below the window_slow SMA (death cross). This is a momentum-driven exit signal, indicating a transition from bullish to bearish momentum. Common periods: 9/21 (short-term), 50/200 (long-term). Adjust for crypto's 24/7 markets. Note: This is a backwards-compatible wrapper around sma_crossover.

props.formula: sma(window_fast)[t-1] >= sma(window_slow)[t-1] and sma(window_fast)[t] < sma(window_slow)[t]

fired.description: True if bearish crossover detected in the current bar, False otherwise

atoms.title: sma_cross_up
atoms.summary: Detect a bullish SMA crossover as an entry signal. Returns True when the window_fast SMA crosses above the window_slow SMA (golden cross). This is a momentum-driven entry signal, indicating a transition from bearish to bullish momentum. Common periods: 9/21 (short-term), 50/200 (long-term). Adjust for crypto's 24/7 markets. Note: This is a backwards-compatible wrapper around sma_crossover.

props.formula: sma(window_fast)[t-1] <= sma(window_slow)[t-1] and sma(window_fast)[t] > sma(window_slow)[t]

fired.description: True if bullish crossover detected in the current bar, False otherwise

atoms.title: sma_crossover
atoms.summary: Detect an SMA crossover signal with configurable direction (bullish or bearish). Uses SMA indicator to calculate window_fast and window_slow SMAs. Returns True when a crossover is detected in the specified direction. Bullish crossover (golden cross): window_fast SMA crosses above window_slow SMA Bearish crossover (death cross): window_fast SMA crosses below window_slow SMA The crossover detection compares the previous and current bars: - Bullish: prev window_fast <= prev window_slow AND current window_fast > current window_slow - Bearish: prev window_fast >= prev window_slow AND current window_fast < current window_slow Common periods: 9/21 (short-term), 50/200 (long-term). Adjust for crypto's 24/7 markets.

props.formula: direction == 'bullish': sma(window_fast)[t-1] <= sma(window_slow)[t-1] and sma(window_fast)[t] > sma(window_slow)[t]; direction == 'bearish': sma(window_fast)[t-1] >= sma(window_slow)[t-1] and sma(window_fast)[t] < sma(window_slow)[t]

fired.description: True if crossover detected in the specified direction, False otherwise

atoms.title: smma_cross_down
atoms.summary: Detect a bearish SMMA crossover (fast SMMA crosses below slow SMMA). Slower, more stable crossover than EMA cross; fewer false triggers.

props.formula: smma(window_fast)[t-1] >= smma(window_slow)[t-1] and smma(window_fast)[t] < smma(window_slow)[t]

fired.description: True if bearish SMMA crossover detected on the current bar

atoms.title: smma_cross_up
atoms.summary: Detect a bullish SMMA crossover (fast SMMA crosses above slow SMMA). Slower, more stable crossover than EMA cross; fewer false triggers.

props.formula: smma(window_fast)[t-1] <= smma(window_slow)[t-1] and smma(window_fast)[t] > smma(window_slow)[t]

fired.description: True if bullish SMMA crossover detected on the current bar

atoms.title: spinning_top_trigger

props.formula: range[t] > 0 and body[t] <= range[t] * body_max and upper_wick[t] >= range[t] * wick_min and lower_wick[t] >= range[t] * wick_min

high.description: highest price traded during the bar

low.description: lowest price traded during the bar

wick_min.description: Minimum wick-to-range ratio for both wicks

fired.description: True if spinning top detected on current bar, False otherwise

notes: Interpretation: Indecision, similar to doji but with a small body. Less significant than doji.
props.source_wording: Small body with upper and lower wicks of similar length.

atoms.title: tema_cross_up
atoms.summary: Detect a bullish TEMA crossover (fast TEMA crosses above slow TEMA). Very low-lag cross signal; expect more whipsaw in noisy markets.

props.formula: tema(window_fast)[t-1] <= tema(window_slow)[t-1] and tema(window_fast)[t] > tema(window_slow)[t]

fired.description: True if bullish TEMA crossover detected on the current bar

atoms.title: three_black_crows_trigger
atoms.summary: Check if three black crows pattern completed on the current bar. Three consecutive bearish candles with lower closes, each opening within the previous body. Strong bearish signal.

props.formula: all three bars bearish, each closing lower than the last, each opening inside the prior body, and every body >= its own range * min_body_ratio

high.description: highest price traded during the bar

low.description: lowest price traded during the bar

fired.description: True if three black crows detected on current bar, False otherwise

props.explanation: Each opens within previous body, closes near low Strong bearish momentum / reversal
props.source_wording: Three consecutive bearish candles

atoms.title: three_inside_down_trigger
atoms.summary: Check if three inside down pattern completed on the current bar. Bullish candle, bearish harami, then bearish close below first candle's open. Confirmed bearish reversal.

props.formula: close[t-2] > open[t-2] and close[t-1] < open[t-1] and open[t-1] < close[t-2] and close[t-1] > open[t-2] and close[t] < open[t] and close[t] < open[t-2]

fired.description: True if three inside down detected on current bar, False otherwise

notes: 2. Bearish candle that forms inside bar
3. Bearish candle that closes below first candle's low
props.source_wording: 1. Bullish candle

atoms.title: three_inside_up_trigger
atoms.summary: Check if three inside up pattern completed on the current bar. Bearish candle, bullish harami, then bullish close above first candle's open. Confirmed bullish reversal.

props.formula: close[t-2] < open[t-2] and close[t-1] > open[t-1] and open[t-1] > close[t-2] and close[t-1] < open[t-2] and close[t] > open[t] and close[t] > open[t-2]

fired.description: True if three inside up detected on current bar, False otherwise

notes: 2. Bullish candle that forms inside bar
3. Bullish candle that closes above first candle's high
props.source_wording: 1. Bearish candle

atoms.title: three_white_soldiers_trigger
atoms.summary: Check if three white soldiers pattern completed on the current bar. Three consecutive bullish candles with higher closes, each opening within the previous body. Strong bullish signal.

props.formula: all three bars bullish, each closing higher than the last, each opening inside the prior body, and every body >= its own range * min_body_ratio

high.description: highest price traded during the bar

low.description: lowest price traded during the bar

fired.description: True if three white soldiers detected on current bar, False otherwise

props.explanation: Each opens within previous body, closes near high Strong bullish momentum / reversal

atoms.title: ttm_squeeze_active
atoms.summary: Check if the Bollinger Bands are inside the Keltner Channel (the squeeze is on). `squeeze_depth` is how far inside the Keltner Channel the narrower Bollinger band sits, so a positive depth IS the squeeze. The indicator measures the distance; this decides that a positive distance counts.

props.usage_example: RuleRegistry.evaluate({'name': 'ttm_squeeze_active', 'params': {'bb_window': value, 'bb_std': value, 'kc_window': value, 'kc_atr_mult': value, 'mom_window': value}}, df)
props.formula: squeeze_depth[t] > 0 -- Bollinger Bands entirely inside the Keltner Channel

high.description: highest price traded during the bar

low.description: lowest price traded during the bar

fired.description: True if squeeze_depth > 0

atoms.title: ttm_squeeze_fired_bearish
atoms.summary: Detect a squeeze releasing with negative momentum. Mirror of `ttm_squeeze_fired_bullish`.

props.usage_example: RuleRegistry.evaluate({'name': 'ttm_squeeze_fired_bearish', 'params': {'bb_window': value, 'bb_std': value, 'kc_window': value, 'kc_atr_mult': value, 'mom_window': value}}, df)
props.formula: squeeze_depth[t-1] > 0 and squeeze_depth[t] <= 0 and momentum[t] < 0

high.description: highest price traded during the bar

low.description: lowest price traded during the bar

fired.description: True on the bar the squeeze releases with momentum < 0

atoms.title: ttm_squeeze_fired_bullish
atoms.summary: Detect a squeeze releasing with positive momentum. The release is `squeeze_depth` crossing down through zero -- the Bollinger bands leaving the Keltner channel. Direction comes from Carter's momentum on the same bar.

props.usage_example: RuleRegistry.evaluate({'name': 'ttm_squeeze_fired_bullish', 'params': {'bb_window': value, 'bb_std': value, 'kc_window': value, 'kc_atr_mult': value, 'mom_window': value}}, df)
props.formula: squeeze_depth[t-1] > 0 and squeeze_depth[t] <= 0 and momentum[t] > 0

high.description: highest price traded during the bar

low.description: lowest price traded during the bar

fired.description: True on the bar the squeeze releases with momentum > 0

atoms.title: tweezer_bottoms_trigger
atoms.summary: Check if a tweezer bottoms pattern completed on the current bar. Two consecutive candles with approximately equal lows, first bearish and second bullish. Bullish reversal.

props.formula: abs(low[t] - low[t-1]) <= mean(range) over the trailing 14 bars * tolerance and close[t-1] < open[t-1] and close[t] > open[t]

high.description: highest price traded during the bar

low.description: lowest price traded during the bar

tolerance.description: Maximum low-to-low difference as fraction of average range

fired.description: True if tweezer bottoms detected on current bar, False otherwise

notes: Price rejection at same level twice indicates strong support/resistance.
Matching lows after downtrend - bullish reversal
props.source_wording: Two or more candles with matching highs (tops) or lows (bottoms).

atoms.title: tweezer_tops_trigger
atoms.summary: Check if a tweezer tops pattern completed on the current bar. Two consecutive candles with approximately equal highs, first bullish and second bearish. Bearish reversal.

props.formula: abs(high[t] - high[t-1]) <= mean(range) over the trailing 14 bars * tolerance and close[t-1] > open[t-1] and close[t] < open[t]

high.description: highest price traded during the bar

low.description: lowest price traded during the bar

tolerance.description: Maximum high-to-high difference as fraction of average range

fired.description: True if tweezer tops detected on current bar, False otherwise

notes: Price rejection at same level twice indicates strong support/resistance.
Matching highs after uptrend - bearish reversal
props.source_wording: Two or more candles with matching highs (tops) or lows (bottoms).

atoms.title: two_bar_reversal_bearish_trigger
atoms.summary: Check if a bearish two-bar reversal completed on the current bar. Bullish bar followed by bearish bar that takes out the high then closes below the prior open. The close_proximity parameter controls how close the close must be to the high/low extreme.

props.formula: close[t-1] > open[t-1] and (high[t-1] - close[t-1]) <= range[t-1] * close_proximity and close[t] < open[t] and (close[t] - low[t]) <= range[t] * close_proximity and high[t] >= high[t-1] and close[t] < open[t-1]

high.description: highest price traded during the bar

low.description: lowest price traded during the bar

close_proximity.description: How close the close must be to the extreme, as a fraction of range. Lower is stricter

fired.description: True if bearish two-bar reversal detected, False otherwise

atoms.title: two_bar_reversal_bullish_trigger
atoms.summary: Check if a bullish two-bar reversal completed on the current bar. Bearish bar followed by bullish bar that takes out the low then closes above the prior open. The close_proximity parameter controls how close the close must be to the high/low extreme.

props.formula: close[t-1] < open[t-1] and (close[t-1] - low[t-1]) <= range[t-1] * close_proximity and close[t] > open[t] and (high[t] - close[t]) <= range[t] * close_proximity and low[t] <= low[t-1] and close[t] > open[t-1]

high.description: highest price traded during the bar

low.description: lowest price traded during the bar

close_proximity.description: How close the close must be to the extreme, as a fraction of range. Lower is stricter

fired.description: True if bullish two-bar reversal detected, False otherwise

atoms.title: ve_above_upper
atoms.summary: Check if close is at or above the volatility envelope's upper band. Today's close is at least `multiplier` standard deviations above YESTERDAY's close, where the deviation is measured on recent returns. The envelope is centred on the previous close, not the current bar -- the old wording said "above the current bar", which would make the comparison vacuous. A STATE, not an event: true for every bar close stays at or beyond the band.

props.formula: close[t] >= vstop_hband[t]

multiplier.description: Stdev multiplier for the band distance

fired.description: True if close >= vstop_hband, False otherwise

atoms.title: ve_below_lower
atoms.summary: Check if close is at or below the volatility envelope's lower band. Mirror of `ve_above_upper`: today's close is at least `multiplier` standard deviations below yesterday's. A STATE, not an event.

props.formula: close[t] <= vstop_lband[t]

multiplier.description: Stdev multiplier for the band distance

fired.description: True if close <= vstop_lband, False otherwise

atoms.title: chart pattern
atoms.summary: A price formation spanning a variable number of bars, identified from swing highs and lows rather than over a fixed window.

props.explanation: Multi-bar formations: head and shoulders, double tops and bottoms, triangles, wedges, flags and pennants, cup and handle, and the necklines and completion criteria that define them. Also pattern reliability and failure modes, and the context a formation requires to mean anything. Sibling of the existing pattern class, not a parent of it and not the same thing. That class holds candlestick geometry -- shapes computable from one bar or a small fixed number of them, which is why 41 signals implement it. A chart pattern needs a swing structure of unknown length, and no computation in the library produces swing points, so this class carries no procedures. It is the first class in the graph that is knowledge without an implementation.
props.source_wording: Chart patterns are recognizable price formations that develop over multiple bars or candles, representing periods of consolidation, accumulation, distribution, or continuation. They provide structure for entries, stops, and targets.
applications: Context is King: Patterns mean nothing without proper context
Confirmation Required: Wait for patterns to complete and confirm
Manage Failures: Plan for pattern failures; they create opportunities
Combine Methods: Use patterns with indicators, volume, and structure
Keep Statistics: Track your success rate with different patterns
Specialize: Master a few patterns rather than superficially knowing many
notes: Technical pattern recognition is both an art and a science. Key takeaways:
Pattern trading success comes from disciplined application of well-defined criteria, not from memorizing hundreds of formations.

chapter_variants.explanation: This document provides a comprehensive reference for technical chart patterns used in trading, including candlestick patterns, multi-bar formations, and classical chart patterns. Pattern recognition is a core skill for discretionary and systematic traders alike.

atoms.title: market foundations
atoms.summary: How a market produces a price: who participates, how their orders meet, and what crossing the spread costs.

props.explanation: Market microstructure, order types, participant classes, liquidity and its price -- slippage and market impact -- volatility regimes and the shifts between them, trading venues and their execution models, bid-ask spread dynamics, and price discovery. This is the layer every computation in the graph silently assumes. An indicator consumes a price series; this subject area is where that series comes from.
applications: Execute efficiently by minimizing transaction costs and market impact
Manage risk by understanding liquidity constraints and volatility dynamics
Develop robust strategies that account for realistic market conditions
Adapt to changing conditions by recognizing regime shifts and adjusting accordingly
notes: Market foundations provide the essential infrastructure knowledge required for systematic trading. Understanding market microstructure, order types, participant dynamics, liquidity conditions, volatility regimes, and venue characteristics enables traders to:
These foundational concepts underpin all advanced trading strategies and should be thoroughly understood before proceeding to instrument-specific mechanics and trading methodologies.

chapter_variants.explanation: This document covers the fundamental concepts underlying financial markets, including market structure, order mechanics, participant dynamics, and execution considerations essential for systematic trading.

atoms.title: market mechanics
atoms.summary: The instruments themselves and the rules under which a position is opened, financed and settled.

props.explanation: Spot markets, futures and perpetual swaps, options, margin and leverage and the liquidation engines that enforce them, crypto-specific mechanics, FX basics, settlement and clearing, and contract specifications. Distinct from market foundations: that subject area covers how a price forms, this one covers what is actually being traded and under whose rules.
applications: Capital Efficiency: Leverage availability varies dramatically across instruments
Risk Profile: Options offer defined risk; futures have unlimited downside
Settlement: Timing and method of settlement impacts cash management
Costs: Transaction costs, funding rates, and carry vary by instrument
Liquidity: Market depth and trading hours affect execution quality
notes: Understanding instruments and market mechanics is fundamental to successful trading. Each instrument type has unique characteristics affecting:
Traders should match instrument selection to their strategy requirements, risk tolerance, and operational capabilities. Master the mechanics before deploying capital.

chapter_variants.explanation: This document covers the various financial instruments available for trading and the specific mechanics governing each market type, including derivatives, leverage, and crypto-specific considerations.

atoms.title: price action
atoms.summary: Reading a market from the shape of its price alone -- structure, levels and regime -- without computing an indicator over it.

props.explanation: Price action theory, market structure, trend versus range and compression versus expansion, liquidity theory, volume and order flow, support and resistance, supply and demand zones, multi-timeframe analysis, confluence, fair value gaps, and volume profile. Deliberately kept beside technical analysis rather than beneath it. Technical analysis is organised in this graph by what a computation *measures*, and its six subclasses are exactly those characters; price action names conclusions drawn from price geometry rather than a character a computation measures, so placing it there would misuse that axis.
notes: Before diving into technical concepts, traders must internalize foundational truths that govern market behavior and strategy selection.
Core trading concepts provide the analytical framework for interpreting market behavior. These concepts are interconnected:
Master these concepts individually, then synthesize them into a cohesive analytical approach that matches your trading style and timeframe.
applications: Identifying entry and exit points based on candlestick patterns
Determining trend direction from swing highs and lows
Finding support and resistance levels from historical price reactions
Reading market sentiment through bar-by-bar analysis
Scalping and day trading without indicator lag
Price Action reveals the story of buyer/seller conflict
Market Structure defines the trend framework
Trend/Range Analysis determines strategy selection
Liquidity Theory explains where price is attracted
Volume Analysis confirms or questions price moves
Support/Resistance identifies key decision points
Supply/Demand locates institutional footprints
Multi-Timeframe Analysis provides context hierarchy
Confluence filters for highest probability setups
Fair Value Gaps identify rebalancing opportunities
Volume Profile & Auction Theory reveals institutional activity and fair value
props.source_wording: Price action is a trading methodology that analyzes pure price movement on charts without relying on lagging indicators. It focuses on reading candles, bars, and price patterns to understand market psychology and predict future price direction based on historical price behavior.
examples: Bullish Price Action: Higher highs and higher lows forming Strong closes near candle highs (buyer dominance) Rejection wicks at support levels Volume confirmation on up moves
Bearish Price Action: Lower highs and lower lows forming Strong closes near candle lows (seller dominance) Rejection wicks at resistance levels Volume confirmation on down moves
Reversal Price Action: Long wick candles (hammer, shooting star) Engulfing patterns at key levels Failure to make new highs/lows Climactic volume at extremes

chapter_variants.explanation: This document covers the fundamental analytical frameworks and concepts used by traders to interpret market behavior, identify opportunities, and make trading decisions.

atoms.title: quantitative analysis
atoms.summary: Statistical structure in returns: what persists, what reverts, and over what horizon.

props.explanation: Seasonality and time-of-day effects, volatility clustering, mean reversion, breakout behaviour, autocorrelation and momentum persistence, machine-learned patterns, cross-sectional versus time-series effects, and carry. Where technical analysis classifies a computation by what it measures, this subject area is about the properties of the series being measured -- the evidence that a given class of computation has anything to find.
applications: Seasonality: Exploit predictable calendar-based effects
Volatility Clustering: Forecast and adapt to volatility regimes
Mean Reversion: Trade deviations from equilibrium
Breakouts: Capture trend initiations and continuations
Momentum: Ride persistent price trends
Machine Learning: Discover complex, non-linear patterns
Cross-Sectional: Exploit relative value differences
Carry: Harvest structural yield premiums
notes: Quantitative patterns provide systematic, data-driven approaches to trading:
Successful quant trading requires rigorous statistical testing, out-of-sample validation, and realistic accounting for transaction costs and market impact.

chapter_variants.explanation: This document covers quantitative patterns and statistical phenomena exploited in systematic trading strategies, including seasonality effects, volatility dynamics, mean reversion signals, and machine learning approaches.

atoms.title: risk management
atoms.summary: Bounding loss: how much to put on, when to stop, and what the portfolio can survive.

props.explanation: Risk dimensions in strategy design, trading rules and protocols, position sizing, drawdown controls, stop-loss and take-profit engineering, portfolio risk, capital efficiency, risk-reward ratios, risk of ruin, and scenario analysis. Signals decide whether to act; this subject area decides at what size and under what limits, and it constrains a strategy independently of which signals it composes.
notes: Before implementing specific risk controls, traders must understand that **risk is multi-dimensional**. Focusing on one dimension while ignoring others leads to false confidence.
Risk management is the foundation of sustainable trading success:
The First Rule of Trading: Preserve capital. You cannot recover from total loss.
The Second Rule: See Rule One.
Successful traders are not those who never lose, but those who manage losses so they can continue trading and capitalize on future opportunities.
applications: Position Sizing: Risk appropriate amounts per trade
Drawdown Controls: Protect against cumulative losses
Stop-Loss Engineering: Balance protection against whipsaws
Portfolio Risk: Manage aggregate exposure and correlation
Capital Efficiency: Deploy capital wisely
Risk-Reward: Ensure favorable trade mathematics
Risk of Ruin: Ensure long-term survival
Scenario Analysis: Prepare for adverse conditions

chapter_variants.explanation: This document covers comprehensive risk management principles and techniques essential for preserving capital and achieving sustainable trading performance. Risk management is the foundation upon which all successful trading is built.

atoms.title: strategy design
atoms.summary: Turning a claim about market behaviour into rules an engine can run, and finding out whether the claim survives contact with data.

props.explanation: Trading styles and the cadence they imply, the archetypes that say why a trade has edge, the trade plan that writes both down, entry and exit logic, time and regime filters, data quality, and the backtesting, walk-forward and validation procedures a strategy has to pass before it is believed. Signals decide what is true of a bar; this subject area decides which signals to compose, in what role, and under what evidence the composition may be trusted.
applications: Clear separation of style, archetype, and signal - Know when you trade vs. why you trade
Explicit alignment between market behavior and strategy logic - Match archetypes to regimes
Understanding of risk profiles - Win rate alone is misleading; skew determines survivability
Regime-aware deployment - Don't apply mean reversion in trends or trend following in ranges
Robust execution and exits - Entry is less important than risk management
Rigorous validation and skepticism - Assume strategies don't work until proven otherwise
props.caution: Critical Insight: Strategies do not fail randomly - they fail when applied to the wrong market behavior. Mean reversion in a trend will blow up. Trend following in a range will bleed out. Know your archetype's risk profile and contraindications.
notes: Effective strategy design requires:

chapter_variants.explanation: This document covers the principles and methodologies for designing, developing, and validating systematic trading strategies, from initial concept through backtesting to deployment.

atoms.title: market microstructure
atoms.summary: The study of how the specific rules, protocols and institutional arrangements of a market turn orders into trades and trades into prices.

applications: Designing execution algorithms that minimize transaction costs by understanding order book dynamics
Analyzing the impact of large trades on market prices before execution
Identifying informed trading activity through order flow analysis
Optimizing order placement and timing based on microstructure patterns
Detecting market manipulation or unusual trading patterns
props.source_wording: Market microstructure is the study of the processes and mechanisms through which securities are traded, including the dynamics of order flow, price formation, transaction costs, and the behavior of market participants. It examines how the specific trading rules, protocols, and institutional arrangements of a market affect trading outcomes.
props.explanation: It is a field rather than a market object, and the chapter opens with it because everything below is one of its subjects: [[Price Discovery]], [[Order Flow]], [[Information Asymmetry]], [[Transaction Costs]] and [[Market Efficiency]]. Its practical claim is that the venue's design changes the outcome, so two identical strategies on two venues do not earn the same amount.

atoms.title: price discovery
atoms.summary: The process by which a market price is determined, as buyers and sellers interact and their orders are continuously matched.

notes: The process by which market prices are determined through the interaction of supply and demand, facilitated by the continuous matching of buy and sell orders
applications: Identifying which market or venue leads price discovery
Understanding how information flows into prices
Timing trades around information events
Designing strategies that exploit slow price discovery
Evaluating market efficiency
examples: Information Events: Earnings announcements: Large discrete price adjustments Economic data releases: Rapid repricing across multiple assets Central bank decisions: Regime-changing price discovery
props.source_wording: Price discovery is the process by which market prices are determined through the interaction of buyers and sellers. It encompasses the mechanisms through which information is incorporated into prices, reflecting the collective assessment of an asset's value.
props.explanation: Prices are not announced, they are discovered. Each match moves the price a little, so the sequence of trades is the mechanism by which dispersed information becomes one number. It runs through [[Auction-Based Discovery]] at the open and close, [[Continuous Trading Discovery]] during the session, and [[Cross-Market Discovery]] between related instruments. How fast it works is what [[Market Efficiency]] measures.

atoms.title: order flow
atoms.summary: The sequence and volume of buy and sell orders arriving at a market, which is what drives price over short horizons.

props.explanation: Flow is directional information before it is price: a run of buy orders consumes the offers and lifts the quote. Because the size and sequence of orders reveals intent, flow is both the raw material of [[Price Discovery]] and the reason [[Information Leakage]] costs money. [[Market Impact]] is what your own contribution to the flow does to the price you get.

atoms.title: information asymmetry
atoms.summary: The unequal distribution of information among participants, where some know more about an asset's value than the person on the other side of their trade.

props.source_wording: The unequal distribution of information among market participants, where some traders possess superior information about asset values
props.explanation: It is the reason a quote is not free. A [[Market Makers]] cannot tell an informed counterparty from an uninformed one, so it widens the [[Bid-Ask Spread]] to cover the losses it will take against the informed ones. Every participant class in the chapter sits somewhere on this gradient, which is what makes [[Market Participants]] worth classifying at all.

atoms.title: transaction costs
atoms.summary: The total cost of trading: explicit costs such as commissions and fees, plus implicit costs such as the spread, market impact and timing.

props.explanation: The implicit half is usually the larger one and is invisible on a statement. Crossing the [[Bid-Ask Spread]] is a cost, [[Slippage]] is a cost, and [[Market Impact]] is a cost you inflict on yourself. A strategy evaluated without them is being measured against a market that does not exist.

atoms.title: market efficiency
atoms.summary: The degree to which prices already reflect the available information, set by how fast and how accurately price discovery works.

props.explanation: Efficiency is a matter of degree and speed rather than a yes or no. It depends on market structure: fragmented venues, wide spreads and thin books all slow the incorporation of information. [[Arbitrageurs]] are the participants whose trading enforces it, and [[Price Discovery]] is the process it grades.

atoms.title: effective spread
atoms.summary: Twice the distance between the trade price and the midpoint at the time -- the spread actually paid.

props.formula: Effective Spread = 2 * |Trade Price - Midpoint Price|
notes: Effective Spread = 2 * |Trade Price - Midpoint|
props.source_wording: The quantity effective spread (measures actual execution cost).
props.explanation: It measures the cost that was really incurred rather than the one advertised, and it differs from [[Quoted Spread]] whenever a trade fills inside the quote or walks through it. It is the honest input to a [[Transaction Costs]] calculation.

atoms.title: price impact (kyle lambda)
atoms.summary: The quantity price impact (kyle lambda).

props.formula: Delta_P = lambda * Order_Flow

order_flow.description: signed order flow over the interval

lam.description: market price sensitivity to order flow (Kyle lambda)

atoms.title: quoted spread
atoms.summary: Ask minus bid -- the spread as displayed, before anyone trades.

props.formula:
Quoted Spread = Ask Price - Bid Price
Relative Spread = (Ask - Bid) / Midpoint * 100%
notes: Quoted Spread = Ask - Bid
props.source_wording: The quantity quoted spread.
props.explanation: It is the headline number and the one that overstates what a patient trader pays, since a limit order need not cross it at all. Expressed as a fraction of the midpoint it becomes comparable across instruments at different price levels.

bid.description: highest price a buyer will pay

ask.description: lowest price a seller will accept

atoms.title: order types
atoms.summary: The instructions a trader gives a market about how a trade should be executed: what price is acceptable, when it should trigger, and how much of it to reveal.

props.source_wording: Order types are specific instructions traders use to communicate with the market about how they want their trades to be executed. Each order type defines the conditions under which a trade should occur, including price constraints, timing, and execution preferences.
props.explanation: Every order type buys one thing at the price of another. [[Market Order]] buys certainty of execution with uncertainty of price; [[Limit Order]] does the reverse. [[Stop Order]] and [[Stop-Limit Order]] add a trigger condition; [[Trailing Stop]] moves that trigger with the price; [[Iceberg Order]] buys concealment with queue position. Choosing among them is choosing which risk to keep.

atoms.title: information leakage
atoms.summary: The extent to which an order reveals a trader's intentions to the rest of the market before it is finished.

props.source_wording: Some order types reveal trading intentions more than others
props.explanation: Order types differ in how much they leak, and the difference is priced: once other participants can infer that size is coming, they move ahead of it and the remaining fills get worse. [[Iceberg Order]] and [[Dark Pools]] are the two answers the chapter gives, one hiding size in a lit book and the other moving the order off it. Leakage is the mechanism by which [[Information Asymmetry]] turns into a cost you pay.

atoms.title: market order
atoms.summary: An instruction to trade immediately at the best price currently available.

examples: Buy 100 shares at the best available price
Result: Immediate fill at current ask price(s), guaranteed execution, uncertain price
applications: Immediate execution when speed is critical (news events, closing positions urgently)
props.explanation: Execution is certain and the price is not: the order walks the book until it is filled, so in a thin market the average fill can be far from the quote. It is the order type that pays the full [[Bid-Ask Spread]] and generates the most [[Slippage]], which is why the chapter advises using it only when speed genuinely matters. A triggered [[Stop Order]] becomes one of these.

atoms.title: limit order
atoms.summary: An instruction to trade only at a stated price or better.

examples: Buy 100 shares at $50 or better
Result: Only fills at $50 or below, may not execute if price never reaches $50
applications: Entering or exiting positions at desired prices, providing liquidity
props.explanation: The price is certain and execution is not. While it rests unfilled it is displayed liquidity that someone else can trade against, which makes the limit order the instrument by which ordinary participants supply [[Liquidity]] rather than consume it. It is also how a trader avoids paying the whole [[Bid-Ask Spread]].

atoms.title: stop order (stop-loss)
atoms.summary: A resting instruction that becomes a market order once the price reaches a trigger level.

examples: Sell 100 shares if price drops to $45
Result: Becomes a market order when price touches $45, then executes at best available
applications: Protecting positions from adverse moves, triggering entries on breakouts
props.explanation: The trigger is certain; the fill is not, because once triggered it is a [[Market Order]] and takes whatever the book offers. In a fast market that gap can be large, which is the failure mode the chapter warns about. Used below a position it caps loss, used above it enters on a breakout.

atoms.title: stop-limit order
atoms.summary: A stop order that becomes a limit order rather than a market order when triggered.

examples: Sell 100 shares if price drops to $45, but not below $44
Result: Triggers at $45, but only fills at $44 or better (may not fill in fast markets)
applications: Combining stop triggers with price limits to avoid poor fills
props.explanation: It bounds the fill price at the cost of possibly not filling at all -- exactly the risk a plain [[Stop Order]] avoids and exactly the protection it lacks. The chapter recommends it in volatile conditions, where the distance a triggered market order can travel is largest.

atoms.title: trailing stop
atoms.summary: A stop whose trigger level follows the price at a fixed distance, moving only in the favourable direction.

examples: Sell if price drops $2 from its highest point since order placed
Result: Stop level adjusts upward as price rises, locks in gains
applications: Locking in profits while allowing positions to run
props.explanation: It converts a static exit into a ratchet: as the position gains, the stop rises behind it and locks in part of the move, but it never retreats. The distance is the whole design decision, and setting it from [[Volatility]] rather than from a round percentage is what makes it survive normal noise.

atoms.title: iceberg order
atoms.summary: A large order that displays only part of its size at a time, refreshing the visible slice as each one fills, so the book never shows how much is really there.

examples: Buy 10,000 shares but only display 500 at a time
Result: Hides true order size to minimize market impact
props.explanation: Showing full size is itself information: a resting order for ten thousand shares tells everyone a large buyer is present and roughly what they will pay, and the market prices that before the order is done. The iceberg withholds it. The cost is queue position, since each refreshed slice goes to the back of its price level, so it trades speed for concealment. It exists to reduce [[Information Leakage]] and with it [[Market Impact]].

atoms.title: market participants
atoms.summary: The individuals, institutions and firms buying and selling in a market, each with distinct motives, time horizons and information.

applications: Identifying which participant types are active to anticipate market behavior
Understanding the "food chain" of market participants to avoid being exploited
Analyzing institutional order flow for directional signals
Recognizing market maker behavior patterns around key levels
props.source_wording: Market participants are individuals, institutions, or entities engaged in the buying and selling of financial instruments within a market. Each participant type has distinct motivations, time horizons, information sets, and trading behaviors that collectively shape market dynamics.
props.explanation: The chapter's claim is that who is trading changes how the market behaves. Motives differ -- speculation, hedging, liquidity provision, arbitrage -- and so do horizons, from the microseconds of [[High-Frequency Traders]] to the years of [[Institutional Investors]]. The relationship is adversarial in one direction only: informed participants profit from uninformed ones, which is [[Information Asymmetry]] seen from the participant side.

atoms.title: retail traders
atoms.summary: Individuals trading their own accounts, typically in small size and over longer holding periods.

props.source_wording: Individual investors trading for personal accounts Typically smaller position sizes, longer holding periods Often use technical analysis, may exhibit behavioral biases Tend to be net liquidity takers
props.explanation: They tend to be net takers of [[Liquidity]] rather than providers of it, and they lean on technical analysis and are prone to behavioural bias. Their size rarely causes [[Market Impact]], which means the costs that dominate for them are the [[Bid-Ask Spread]] and [[Slippage]] rather than the impact of their own flow.

atoms.title: institutional investors
atoms.summary: Mutual funds, pension funds, insurance companies and endowments, trading large positions on long horizons.

props.source_wording: Mutual funds, pension funds, insurance companies, endowments Large position sizes requiring careful execution over time Focus on fundamental analysis, longer time horizons Create significant market impact when repositioning
props.explanation: Size is their defining constraint: a position large enough to matter is large enough to move the price, so execution has to be spread over time. That is what makes [[Market Impact]] their central cost and why [[Dark Pools]] and schedule algorithms like [[VWAP]] exist. Their repositioning is visible in volume patterns, which is why other participants watch for it.

atoms.title: market makers
atoms.summary: Participants who quote both sides continuously, earning the spread in exchange for standing ready to trade.

props.source_wording: Provide continuous two-sided quotes (bid and ask) Profit from the bid-ask spread while managing inventory risk Obligated to provide liquidity in exchange markets Use sophisticated algorithms to manage quotes and hedge exposure
props.explanation: The [[Bid-Ask Spread]] is their compensation for two risks: holding inventory that may fall in value, and trading against someone who knows more. They widen the quote when they suspect the second, which is why spreads open up around uncertainty. Competition among them is what narrows the quote back down. In exchange markets the obligation to keep quoting is formal, which makes them the supply side of [[Liquidity]].

atoms.title: high-frequency traders (hft)
atoms.summary: Firms using ultra-low-latency technology to trade on horizons of milliseconds to seconds.

props.source_wording: Use ultra-low latency technology for speed advantage Strategies include market making, arbitrage, latency arbitrage Hold positions for milliseconds to seconds Provide significant liquidity but can withdraw in stress
props.explanation: Speed is the whole edge, applied to market making, arbitrage and latency arbitrage. They supply a great deal of [[Liquidity]] in normal conditions and can withdraw it under stress, which is the [[Liquidity]] illusion the chapter warns about. If an execution schedule is predictable they can trade ahead of it, so predictability is itself [[Information Leakage]].

atoms.title: arbitrageurs
atoms.summary: Participants who exploit price discrepancies between related instruments, generally holding hedged, market-neutral positions.

props.source_wording: Exploit price discrepancies between related instruments ETF-underlying arbitrage, cross-exchange arbitrage, statistical arbitrage Force prices toward efficiency Generally market-neutral with hedged positions
props.explanation: ETF against underlying, one exchange against another, statistical relationships between securities: in each case the trade is the difference rather than the direction. Their activity is the mechanism that forces prices back together, which makes them the enforcers of [[Market Efficiency]] and a driver of [[Cross-Market Discovery]].

atoms.title: hedge funds
atoms.summary: Pooled investment firms running diverse strategies with leverage and shorter horizons than traditional asset managers.

props.source_wording: Pursue diverse strategies: long/short equity, macro, quantitative Aggressive risk-taking with leverage Shorter time horizons than traditional asset managers Can be liquidity providers or aggressive liquidity takers
props.explanation: Long/short equity, macro and quantitative approaches sit under one label, so the category describes a structure rather than a method. They can be either side of the [[Liquidity]] relationship depending on the strategy, providing it when they quote and consuming it aggressively when they need to move.

atoms.title: proprietary trading firms
atoms.summary: Firms trading their own capital, systematically or discretionarily, with no external investors to answer to.

props.source_wording: Trade firm capital using systematic or discretionary strategies Often specialize in specific markets or strategies May operate HFT or longer-term systematic strategies No external investor constraints
props.explanation: The absence of client money removes the constraints that shape [[Institutional Investors]] -- no redemption risk, no mandate, no reporting horizon -- which lets them specialise narrowly. Some operate at the speed of [[High-Frequency Traders]] and others on much longer systematic horizons.

atoms.title: liquidity
atoms.summary: The ease with which an asset can be bought or sold without materially moving its price.

applications: Estimating realistic execution costs for strategy backtesting
Determining optimal order sizing based on available liquidity
Choosing execution algorithms (TWAP, VWAP, Implementation Shortfall)
Identifying low-liquidity periods to avoid or exploit
Stress-testing strategies for liquidity withdrawal scenarios
props.source_wording: Liquidity theory in trading context refers to understanding where resting orders (stop-losses, pending orders) accumulate in the market, and how price tends to seek out these liquidity pools before making significant moves. It explains why markets often "hunt" stops before reversing.
props.explanation: High liquidity shows up as a tight [[Bid-Ask Spread]], a deep book and small [[Market Impact]] -- three symptoms of one condition. It is not constant: it varies by time of day and by regime, and displayed size often disappears when it is tested, so the book overstates what is really available. Everything about execution cost follows from it.
examples: Liquidity Sweep Setup: Identify obvious swing high with clustered stops above Wait for price to spike above high (sweeping liquidity) Look for immediate rejection (long wick, engulfing candle) Enter short with stop above the sweep Target opposing liquidity zone

applications: Avoiding stop-loss placement at obvious levels
Anticipating false breakouts at liquidity zones
Entering trades after liquidity sweeps
Understanding why breakouts fail
Identifying where large players likely accumulate/distribute

atoms.title: slippage
atoms.summary: The difference between the price a trade was expected to get and the price it actually got.

examples: Slippage Example: Expected buy price: $100.00 (midpoint) Market order for 1,000 shares Actual average fill: $100.15 Slippage: $0.15 per share ($150 total)
props.source_wording: The difference between the expected price of a trade and the actual executed price, typically caused by market movement or insufficient liquidity.
props.explanation: It comes from two sources that are worth separating: the market moving while the order works, and the book being too thin to fill it at the quote. The second is [[Liquidity]] and is partly under the trader's control through sizing and timing; the first is not. Because a backtest fills at a price nobody was offering, slippage assumptions are what make simulated results comparable to real ones.

atoms.title: market impact
atoms.summary: The effect a trader's own order has on the price, caused by consuming the liquidity that was there.

examples: Market Impact Example: Order: Buy 50,000 shares of a stock with 100,000 average daily volume Pre-trade price: $50.00 Execution over 2 hours raises price to $50.80 during buying Price settles to $50.50 after completion Temporary impact: $0.30 (reversed) Permanent impact: $0.50 (persisted)
props.explanation: It grows faster than linearly with size, so doubling an order more than doubles the damage -- which is the entire argument for breaking orders up and for [[VWAP]] and [[TWAP]] schedules. Part of it reverses once the order stops (temporary) and part persists because the market has learned something (permanent). Working slower reduces it but exposes the order to price movement, and that trade-off is what [[Implementation Shortfall]] tries to optimise.

atoms.title: simple slippage
atoms.summary: The quantity simple slippage.

props.formula:
Slippage = Actual Execution Price - Expected Price
Slippage % = Slippage / Expected Price * 100%

atoms.title: almgren-chriss market impact model
atoms.summary: Computes almgren-chriss market impact model.

props.formula:
Total Cost = Temporary Impact + Permanent Impact + Volatility Risk

Temporary Impact = eta * sigma * (X/V)^(3/5)
Permanent Impact = gamma * (X/V)

atoms.title: square root market impact rule (empirical)
atoms.summary: The identity square root market impact rule (empirical).

props.formula: Impact = constant * sigma * sqrt(X / V)

atoms.title: participation rate
atoms.summary: Order size as a fraction of the volume traded over the execution window -- how much of the market's activity is you.

props.formula: Participation Rate = Order Size / (ADV * Trading Duration in Days)
props.source_wording: The quantity participation rate.
props.explanation: It is the practical control on [[Market Impact]]: the chapter's guidance is to stay under roughly ten per cent of average daily volume, because impact scales with the share of flow you represent rather than with the absolute size. It is computed as order size divided by average daily volume times the duration in days.

atoms.title: market regimes
atoms.summary: Distinct periods in which volatility, trend behaviour and correlation structure are characteristically different.

props.source_wording: Markets exist in one of three primary states: trending (directional movement), ranging (sideways consolidation), or transitioning between them. Compression refers to decreasing volatility and range contraction, while expansion refers to increasing volatility and range widening.
props.explanation: A regime is a persistent state rather than a mood: markets stay in one until a catalyst moves them, which is why a strategy can work for a year and then stop. The chapter names two by their volatility, [[Low Volatility Regime]] and [[High Volatility Regime]], and correlations behave differently in each -- they compress in calm and converge in stress, so diversification fails exactly when it is needed.
applications: Selecting appropriate trading strategies for current conditions
Anticipating breakouts from compression phases
Identifying trend exhaustion
Setting realistic profit targets based on market state
Filtering trade signals based on trend alignment

atoms.title: regime shifts
atoms.summary: The transition from one market regime to another, triggered by a change in fundamentals, sentiment or structure.

examples: Regime Shift Triggers: Central bank policy changes Geopolitical events Financial crises or credit events Major economic data surprises Structural market changes
props.source_wording: Transitions between different market regimes, often triggered by changes in fundamental conditions, sentiment, or structural factors.
props.explanation: Central bank policy, geopolitics, credit events and data surprises are the usual catalysts. The practical problem is asymmetry of speed: the shift happens faster than any detector recognises it, so a strategy that switches on a detected regime is always switching late. That argues for deciding in advance what to do rather than reacting.

atoms.title: low volatility regime
atoms.summary: A market state of tight ranges and mean-reverting price action, conventionally marked by VIX below 15.

props.source_wording: VIX below 15 Tight trading ranges, mean-reverting price action Low correlations between assets Carry strategies and short volatility strategies perform well Trend-following strategies underperform
props.explanation: Correlations between assets are low, so diversification actually works. Carry and short-volatility strategies do well and trend-following underperforms, because there is no sustained direction to follow. It is the state in which risk looks cheapest and is being accumulated.

atoms.title: high volatility regime
atoms.summary: A market state of large daily moves and persistent direction, conventionally marked by VIX above 25 to 30.

props.source_wording: VIX above 25-30 Large daily moves, trend persistence Elevated correlations (risk-on/risk-off behavior) Momentum and trend-following strategies perform well Mean reversion strategies suffer
props.explanation: Correlations rise together as everything trades risk-on or risk-off, so the diversification that worked in calm stops working. Momentum and trend-following do well and mean reversion suffers. The chapter's guidance is to cut position size and leverage here rather than to change the strategy.

atoms.title: historical volatility (standard deviation of returns)
atoms.summary: The realised dispersion of returns over a window, the standard deviation of returns scaled to a common horizon.

props.formula:
sigma = sqrt(1/(n-1) * sum((r_i - r_bar)^2))

Annualized Vol = Daily Vol * sqrt(252)
props.source_wording: The quantity historical volatility (standard deviation of returns).
props.explanation: It is what volatility actually was, not what it is expected to be, and annualising it by the square root of the number of periods is what makes two windows comparable. Being backward-looking it reacts to a regime change only after the fact, which is the gap [[GARCH]] and [[Volatility Ratio]] try to close.

atoms.title: garch(1,1) model (volatility forecasting)
atoms.summary: A model that forecasts next period's variance from the last shock and the last variance.

props.formula: sigma_t^2 = omega + alpha * epsilon_(t-1)^2 + beta * sigma_(t-1)^2
props.source_wording: Computes garch(1,1) model (volatility forecasting).
props.explanation: It is the formal statement of two facts about [[Volatility]] -- that shocks persist and that variance reverts to a long-run level -- with one parameter for each plus a weight on the long-run term. It is a model you run rather than a quantity you read off the tape, which is what separates it from [[Historical Volatility]].

atoms.title: volatility ratio (regime detection)
atoms.summary: The dispersion of returns for a security or index, conventionally measured as their standard deviation or variance.

props.formula: Vol Ratio = Short-term Vol / Long-term Vol
props.source_wording: The quantity volatility ratio (regime detection).
props.explanation: It behaves in ways that make it forecastable even though returns are not: it clusters, so high volatility follows high volatility; it reverts to a long-run average; and it rises more on down moves than up ones. Those regularities are what [[GARCH]] models. It is measured historically by [[Historical Volatility]], per bar by [[Average True Range]], and its change by [[Volatility Ratio]].

atoms.title: trading venues
atoms.summary: The platforms and marketplaces where instruments trade: exchanges, alternative trading systems and over-the-counter markets.

applications: Routing orders to venues with best price and liquidity
Using dark pools for large orders to minimize information leakage
Accessing specific participant pools (retail, institutional)
Arbitraging price differences across venues
Selecting venues based on fee structures (maker-taker, payment for order flow)
props.explanation: Modern markets are fragmented across many of them, which is why routing is a decision at all. They differ along a transparency spectrum from fully lit to fully dark, in latency, and in the regulation they operate under. Brokers are obliged to seek the best price across them, which is what makes fragmentation tractable rather than chaotic.

atoms.title: execution models
atoms.summary: The methods and protocols by which orders are matched and filled, differing in transparency, speed and who may participate.

props.source_wording: Methods and protocols by which trades are matched and executed, varying by transparency, speed, and participant access.
props.explanation: A venue is where you trade; an execution model is how the match happens once you are there -- continuous price-time priority, periodic auction, dealer quotation, or an algorithm working an order across venues over time. [[TWAP]], [[VWAP]], [[Implementation Shortfall]] and liquidity-seeking algorithms are the schedules the chapter names.

atoms.title: lit exchanges (nyse, nasdaq, lse)
atoms.summary: Venues with full pre-trade transparency: the order book is visible and matching follows price-time priority.

props.source_wording: Full pre-trade transparency (visible order book) Price-time priority for order matching Regulatory oversight and surveillance Best for price discovery and transparent execution
props.explanation: Because everyone can see resting size, they are where [[Price Discovery]] mostly happens -- and for the same reason they are where a large order leaks the most. Regulatory oversight and surveillance are part of the package.

atoms.title: dark pools
atoms.summary: Venues with no pre-trade transparency, where orders stay hidden until they execute.

props.source_wording: No pre-trade transparency (orders hidden until execution) Match large orders without market impact May offer midpoint pricing Used by institutional investors for block trades
props.explanation: The whole point is matching size without announcing it, often at the midpoint, which is why [[Institutional Investors]] use them for block trades. The trade-off is that you cannot see what is there, so execution quality has to be measured after the fact rather than assumed. They solve the same problem as [[Iceberg Order]] by a different route: hiding the order rather than hiding its size.

atoms.title: electronic communication networks (ecns)
atoms.summary: Automated venues that match buy and sell orders directly, often outside standard trading hours.

props.source_wording: Automated matching of buy and sell orders Often offer extended trading hours Direct access without intermediaries Variable fee structures
props.explanation: They give direct access without an intermediary and typically extend the session, which is where early reaction to news happens. Fee structures vary and are worth reading, because on a small spread the fee can exceed it.

atoms.title: over-the-counter (otc) markets
atoms.summary: Bilateral markets where dealers trade directly with each other or with clients rather than through an exchange.

props.source_wording: Direct dealer-to-dealer or dealer-to-client trading Common for bonds, derivatives, FX Customizable contract terms Less standardization, more counterparty risk
props.explanation: Terms are negotiable rather than standardised, which is what makes them the home of bonds, many derivatives and FX. The cost of that flexibility is counterparty risk and less price transparency, since there is no central book to look at.

atoms.title: internalization
atoms.summary: A broker filling a customer order from its own inventory instead of sending it to an exchange.

props.source_wording: Broker fills customer order from own inventory No exchange fees, potentially faster execution Potential conflicts of interest Subject to best execution requirements
props.explanation: It avoids exchange fees and can be faster, and it puts the broker on the other side of its own customer -- which is why best-execution obligations exist and why the practice is scrutinised. The order never reaches a public book, so it contributes nothing to [[Price Discovery]].

atoms.title: twap
atoms.summary: An execution schedule that splits an order evenly across a time window.

props.explanation: It makes no attempt to predict volume: it just spreads participation so no single moment carries the whole order, which limits [[Market Impact]] at the cost of exposure to price drift over the window. Its evenness is also its weakness, since it trades the same amount in thin periods as in thick ones.

atoms.title: vwap
atoms.summary: Matching market volume profile. Executes proportional to volume

atoms.title: implementation shortfall
atoms.summary: An execution schedule that balances market impact against the risk of the price moving while the order works.

props.source_wording: Minimizing total cost. Balances impact vs. timing risk
props.explanation: It is the explicit statement of the urgency-cost trade-off: going fast costs [[Market Impact]], going slow costs drift, and the optimum depends on volatility and order size. Where [[TWAP]] and [[VWAP]] follow a fixed rule, this one solves for a schedule.

atoms.title: sniper/liquidity seeking
atoms.summary: Capturing hidden liquidity. Pings dark pools

atoms.title: bid-ask spread dynamics
atoms.summary: The gap between the highest price a buyer will pay and the lowest a seller will accept -- the price of immediacy.

applications: Measuring transaction costs and market efficiency
Identifying periods of market stress or uncertainty
Comparing liquidity across different assets
Evaluating execution quality
Detecting unusual market conditions
examples: Tight Spread (Liquid Market): Asset: SPY ETF Bid: $450.00 Ask: $450.01 Spread: $0.01 (0.002%) Indication: Highly liquid, low transaction cost
Wide Spread (Illiquid Market): Asset: Small-cap stock Bid: $12.50 Ask: $12.80 Spread: $0.30 (2.4%) Indication: Illiquid, high transaction cost
Spread Widening Event: Normal spread: $0.02 Pre-earnings announcement: $0.08 Post-earnings (uncertainty resolved): $0.02 Interpretation: Market makers charged premium for uncertainty
props.source_wording: The bid-ask spread is the difference between the highest price a buyer is willing to pay (bid) and the lowest price a seller is willing to accept (ask). It represents the cost of immediacy and compensates liquidity providers for their services and risks.
props.explanation: It is what [[Market Makers]] earn for standing ready to trade, and it moves for reasons that are readable. It widens when they fear trading against someone informed, when inventory risk is high, and when [[Volatility]] rises; it narrows when more of them compete. Because it widens under uncertainty, the spread doubles as an indicator of market stress rather than only a cost.

atoms.title: relative spread (percentage)
atoms.summary: The quantity relative spread (percentage).

props.formula:
Relative Spread = (Ask - Bid) / Midpoint * 100%
Midpoint = (Bid + Ask) / 2

bid.description: highest price a buyer will pay

ask.description: lowest price a seller will accept

atoms.title: realized spread (market maker profit after price movement)
atoms.summary: Twice the signed distance between the trade price and the midpoint some interval later -- what the market maker kept.

props.formula: Realized Spread = 2 * D * (Trade Price - Midpoint after t)
props.source_wording: The quantity realized spread (market maker profit after price movement).
props.explanation: Comparing it with [[Effective Spread]] separates the two halves of the spread: what the liquidity provider earned, and what it lost to price movement against it. The difference is the cost of [[Information Asymmetry]], measured rather than assumed.

midpoint_after.description: midpoint a fixed interval after the trade

atoms.title: auction-based discovery
atoms.summary: Price discovery by batching orders and clearing them at a single price, as at the open and close.

props.source_wording: Opening/closing auctions aggregate orders to set a single clearing price Reduces volatility by batching orders Used for price-setting in many equity markets
props.explanation: Aggregating a period's orders into one crossing dampens the volatility that continuous matching produces at those moments, which is why many equity markets set official opening and closing prices this way. The batch is also where the day's largest concentrations of interest meet.

atoms.title: continuous trading discovery
atoms.summary: Price discovery tick by tick, as individual orders match through the session.

props.source_wording: Prices update tick-by-tick as orders match Provides real-time price information Can be noisy in thin markets
props.explanation: It gives a live price at every moment, which is its value, and it is noisy in thin markets, which is its cost -- a single small order can move the print. It is the mode in which most of the session runs, bracketed by [[Auction-Based Discovery]] at each end.

atoms.title: cross-market discovery
atoms.summary: Price discovery that happens between related instruments rather than within one book.

props.source_wording: Futures often lead spot price discovery Options markets embed volatility expectations ADRs and local shares influence each other ETFs and underlying baskets arbitrage to equilibrium
props.explanation: Futures often lead spot, options embed a volatility expectation the underlying does not show, and ETFs and their baskets are pulled together by arbitrage. The consequence is that the price of one instrument carries information about another before that other has moved, which is what lead-lag analysis looks for and what [[Arbitrageurs]] enforce.

atoms.title: information share (hasbrouck)
atoms.summary: The quantity information share (hasbrouck).

props.formula: Information Share = Var(market_i contribution to efficient price) / Var(total efficient price)

variance_contribution.description: variance of this market's contribution to the efficient price

variance_total.description: variance of the total efficient price

atoms.title: component share
atoms.summary: The quantity component share.

props.formula: Component Share = Var(permanent price impact from market_i) / Var(total permanent price impact)

permanent_impact_market.description: permanent price impact from this market

atoms.title: price efficiency ratio
atoms.summary: The quantity price efficiency ratio.

props.formula: Efficiency = Variance(Returns over long horizon) / (n * Variance(Returns over short horizon))

var_long.description: return variance over the long horizon

var_short.description: return variance over the short horizon

atoms.title: core principles
atoms.summary: Things that are true of this market whether or not anyone acts on them. A strategy does not get to disagree with one: it either accounts for it or pays for it.

atoms.title: best practices
atoms.summary: Things we follow because someone has already paid to learn them. Each is a default rather than a rule -- departing from one is often right, but it should be a decision with a reason.

atoms.title: spot markets
atoms.summary: A market where an instrument is bought and sold for immediate delivery at the current price.

applications: Long-term investment and portfolio construction
Basis for derivatives pricing (spot-futures relationships)
Arbitrage between spot and derivative markets
Direct exposure to asset price movements
Dividend capture and income strategies
props.source_wording: Spot markets (also called cash markets) are financial markets where financial instruments are traded for immediate delivery and settlement. The "spot price" represents the current market price at which an asset can be bought or sold for immediate exchange.
props.explanation: What is traded is the asset itself rather than a claim on it later, so there is no expiration to manage and the holder has the full rights of ownership. The spot price is the reference every derivative is priced against, through the [[Cost of Carry Relationship]].

atoms.title: equity spot market
atoms.summary: The market for immediate purchase of shares, conveying ownership of the company.

examples: Purchase 100 shares of AAPL at $175.50 Settlement: T+2 (trade date plus two business days) Ownership: Full shareholder rights, dividends, voting
props.explanation: The buyer receives the full rights of a shareholder -- dividends, votes, corporate actions -- which is the difference between holding stock and holding a derivative on it. Settlement takes two business days.

atoms.title: forex spot market
