atoms.title: confluence score
atoms.summary: The weighted count of independent factors agreeing at one level.

props.formula:
Score = Sum of (Factor_Present * Factor_Weight)

Example weights:
  Major S/R (HTF): 3
  Moving Average (200): 2
  Fibonacci Level: 2
  Trend Line: 2
  Supply/Demand Zone: 2
  Round Number: 1
  Minor S/R (LTF): 1
props.source_wording: The quantity confluence score.
props.explanation: Weighting is what stops five weak agreements outranking one strong one; the chapter's weights put a higher-timeframe level at three and a round number at one.

atoms.title: zone overlap
atoms.summary: The intersection of the individual zones a level is made of.

props.formula:
Confluence Zone = Intersection of all individual zones
High Confluence if Zone_Width < ATR and Factor_Count >= 3
props.source_wording: The quantity zone overlap.
props.explanation: It is what turns several near-agreements into one tradeable area, and it is only high confluence if the overlap is tighter than an [[Average True Range]] and at least three factors are in it.

atoms.title: core principles
atoms.summary: Things that are true of this market whether or not anyone acts on them. A strategy does not get to disagree with one: it either accounts for it or pays for it.

atoms.title: best practices
atoms.summary: Things we follow because someone has already paid to learn them. Each is a default rather than a rule -- departing from one is often right, but it should be a decision with a reason.

atoms.title: trading styles
atoms.summary: Trading styles define the timeframe and execution cadence a trader uses to engage with markets. Trading style is independent of strategy logic and reflects constraints such as available time, attention, and risk tolerance. > Important Distinction: > *Trading style defines when you trade. Strategy archetypes define why a trade has edge.*

atoms.title: scalping
atoms.summary: Trading in seconds to minutes for one to ten ticks at a time, dozens to hundreds of times a day.

props.explanation: The edge per trade is smaller than the [[Bid-Ask Spread]] on most instruments, which is why it needs direct market access, low commissions and the tightest spreads available: costs are not a deduction from the profit here, they are comparable to it. It also needs uninterrupted attention, which is the constraint that rules it out for most traders rather than the strategy logic.
notes: Challenges: High transaction costs, requires constant attention, mentally exhausting.
Best For: Full-time traders with direct market access and low commissions.
Trade duration: Seconds to a few minutes Profit targets: 1-10 ticks/pips High frequency: Dozens to hundreds of trades per day Requires: Fast execution, tight spreads, intense focus
props.key_traits: Tiny moves, high volume, requires intense focus
props.source_wording: Seconds to minutes. Seconds to minutes. Tiny moves, high volume, requires intense focus

atoms.title: day trading
atoms.summary: Trading intraday moves and closing every position before the session ends, typically one to ten trades a day.

props.explanation: Flat at the close means the overnight gap cannot reach the position, and neither can the financing that [[Swap/Rollover Calculation]] measures -- the risk being avoided is the one that arrives while the market is shut and no stop can execute. The cost is that every position must resolve inside a session whether or not the move has finished.
notes: Advantages: No overnight gap risk, fresh start each day, compounds learning quickly.
Best For: Traders who can dedicate market hours to active trading.
Trade duration: Minutes to hours All positions closed by market close No overnight risk exposure Typical trades: 1-10 per day
props.key_traits: Exploit intraday moves, avoid overnight risk
props.source_wording: Minutes to hours. Same day. Exploit intraday moves, avoid overnight risk

atoms.title: swing trading
atoms.summary: Holding for days to weeks to capture a multi-day swing, trading selectively rather than often.

props.explanation: Fewer, larger targets make transaction costs a small share of the gain, which is what lets the style tolerate a lower hit rate. Holding through the close accepts gap risk in exchange for not having to be at the screen, and it is the shortest style that can be run alongside a full-time job.
notes: Advantages: Less screen time, larger profit targets, lower transaction costs as percentage of gains.
Best For: Part-time traders, those seeking work-life balance.
Trade duration: Days to weeks Captures multi-day price swings Fewer trades, higher quality setups Can be done with a full-time job
props.key_traits: Fewer trades, larger moves, higher selectivity
props.source_wording: Days to weeks. Days to weeks. Fewer trades, larger moves, higher selectivity

atoms.title: position trading
atoms.summary: Holding for weeks to months on a regime or fundamental view rather than on a chart event.

props.source_wording: Weeks to months. Weeks to months. Regime- or fundamentally driven
props.explanation: The thesis is about the [[Market Regime]] itself, so the position is sized and stopped against a regime change rather than against a level. It is the only style whose holding period is long enough for carry, financing and correlation to dominate the outcome.

atoms.title: backtesting
atoms.summary: Backtesting is the process of applying a trading strategy to historical data to evaluate how it would have performed. Proper backtesting methodology is critical for realistic performance estimation.

props.backtesting_framework: class Backtester: def __init__(self, data, strategy, capital=100000): self.data = data self.strategy = strategy self.capital = capital self.positions = [] self.equity_curve = [] def run(self): """ Execute backtest """ equity = self.capital position = 0 for i in range(len(self.data)): # Get signal signal = self.strategy.generate_signal(self.data.iloc[:i+1]) # Execute trades with realistic costs if signal != position: trade_cost = self.calculate_costs(position, signal) equity -= trade_cost position = signal # Update equity if position != 0: returns = self.data['returns'].iloc[i] equity *= (1 + position * returns) self.equity_curve.append(equity) return self.calculate_metrics() def calculate_costs(self, old_pos, new_pos): """ Realistic transaction costs """ commission = 0.001  # 0.1% slippage = 0.0005   # 0.05% return abs(new_pos - old_pos) * (commission + slippage) * self.capital ---
props.performance_metric: def calculate_backtest_metrics(returns): """ Standard backtest performance metrics """ metrics = { 'total_return': (1 + returns).prod() - 1, 'annual_return': returns.mean() * 252, 'annual_volatility': returns.std() * np.sqrt(252), 'sharpe_ratio': returns.mean() / returns.std() * np.sqrt(252), 'max_drawdown': calculate_max_drawdown(returns), 'win_rate': (returns > 0).mean(), 'profit_factor': returns[returns > 0].sum() / abs(returns[returns < 0].sum()), 'avg_win': returns[returns > 0].mean(), 'avg_loss': returns[returns < 0].mean(), 'num_trades': count_trades(returns) } return metrics ---

atoms.summary: Realistic cost assumptions by asset class

atoms.title: slippage modeling
atoms.summary: Market impact estimation

props.formula:
def estimate_slippage(trade_size, adv, volatility):
    """
    Market impact estimation
    """
    participation = trade_size / adv
    impact = volatility * np.sqrt(participation) * 0.1
    return impact

atoms.title: walk-forward optimization
atoms.summary: Walk-forward optimization (WFO) is a method for optimizing strategy parameters while avoiding overfitting by repeatedly optimizing on in-sample data and testing on subsequent out-of-sample data.

props.walk_forward_process: def walk_forward_optimization(data, strategy_class, optimization_window=252, test_window=63, param_grid=None): """ Walk-forward optimization framework """ results = [] for i in range(optimization_window, len(data) - test_window, test_window): # In-sample optimization window train_data = data.iloc[i-optimization_window:i] # Out-of-sample test window test_data = data.iloc[i:i+test_window] # Optimize parameters on training data best_params = optimize_parameters(train_data, strategy_class, param_grid) # Test on out-of-sample data strategy = strategy_class(**best_params) oos_returns = strategy.backtest(test_data) results.append({ 'period_start': data.index[i], 'period_end': data.index[i+test_window], 'params': best_params, 'oos_returns': oos_returns, 'oos_sharpe': calculate_sharpe(oos_returns) }) return pd.DataFrame(results) ---

atoms.title: parameter optimization
atoms.summary: Grid search for optimal parameters

props.formula:
from itertools import product

def optimize_parameters(data, strategy_class, param_grid):
    """
    Grid search for optimal parameters
    """
    best_sharpe = -np.inf
    best_params = None
    
    # Generate all parameter combinations
    param_combinations = list(product(*param_grid.values()))
    
    for params in param_combinations:
        param_dict = dict(zip(param_grid.keys(), params))
        
        strategy = strategy_class(**param_dict)
        returns = strategy.backtest(data)
        sharpe = calculate_sharpe(returns)
        
        if sharpe > best_sharpe:
            best_sharpe = sharpe
            best_params = param_dict
    
    return best_params

atoms.title: anchored (expanding window)
atoms.summary: Training window expands over time

props.formula:
def anchored_walk_forward(data, strategy_class, test_window=63):
    """
    Training window expands over time
    """
    min_train = 252
    results = []
    
    for i in range(min_train, len(data) - test_window, test_window):
        # Training: all data from start to i
        train_data = data.iloc[:i]
        test_data = data.iloc[i:i+test_window]
        
        # ... rest of optimization

atoms.title: rolling (fixed window)
atoms.summary: Training window is fixed size

props.formula:
def rolling_walk_forward(data, strategy_class, train_window=252, test_window=63):
    """
    Training window is fixed size
    """
    results = []
    
    for i in range(train_window, len(data) - test_window, test_window):
        # Training: fixed window before i
        train_data = data.iloc[i-train_window:i]
        test_data = data.iloc[i:i+test_window]
        
        # ... rest of optimization

atoms.title: strategy validation
atoms.summary: Strategy validation involves rigorous testing procedures to ensure a strategy has genuine predictive power rather than being an artifact of data mining, overfitting, or statistical flukes.

props.validation_checklist: 1. **Economic Rationale**: Can you explain why the strategy works? 2. **Out-of-Sample Testing**: Does it work on data not used in development? 3. **Statistical Significance**: Are returns significantly different from zero? 4. **Parameter Stability**: Do results hold across parameter variations? 5. **Time Period Stability**: Does it work in different market regimes? 6. **Transaction Costs**: Does it survive realistic costs? 7. **Capacity**: Can it be implemented at desired scale? 8. **Simplicity**: Is the strategy simpler than alternatives? ---

atoms.title: look-ahead bias
atoms.summary: Using information not available at trade time

props.explanation: Prevention: Use only data available at decision point

atoms.title: survivorship bias
atoms.summary: Excluding failed companies/assets from analysis

props.explanation: Prevention: Use point-in-time databases with delisted securities

atoms.title: data snooping bias
atoms.summary: Testing many variations until one works

props.explanation: Prevention: Pre-specify tests, use out-of-sample data

atoms.title: selection bias
atoms.summary: Cherry-picking favorable time periods

props.explanation: Prevention: Test across full available history

atoms.title: overfitting
atoms.summary: Fitting noise rather than signal

props.explanation: Prevention: Use simple models, walk-forward optimization
props.formula:
def walk_forward_validation(features, target, model_class, window=252, step=21):
    """
    Walk-forward validation to avoid look-ahead bias
    """
    results = []
    
    for i in range(window, len(features) - step, step):
        # Train on historical window
        X_train = features.iloc[i-window:i]
        y_train = target.iloc[i-window:i]
        
        # Test on next step
        X_test = features.iloc[i:i+step]
        y_test = target.iloc[i:i+step]
        
        model = model_class()
        model.fit(X_train, y_train)
        
        predictions = model.predict(X_test)
        results.append({
            'start': features.index[i],
            'accuracy': (predictions == y_test).mean(),
            'predictions': predictions
        })
    
    return pd.DataFrame(results)
def analyze_feature_importance(model, feature_names):
    """

atoms.title: t-test for returns
atoms.summary: Test if mean return is significantly different from null

props.formula:
from scipy import stats

def test_significance(returns, null_return=0):
    """
    Test if mean return is significantly different from null
    """
    t_stat, p_value = stats.ttest_1samp(returns, null_return)
    
    return {
        't_statistic': t_stat,
        'p_value': p_value,
        'significant_5pct': p_value < 0.05,
        'significant_1pct': p_value < 0.01
    }

atoms.title: multiple testing correction
atoms.summary: Adjust for multiple hypothesis tests

props.formula:
def bonferroni_correction(p_values, alpha=0.05):
    """
    Adjust for multiple hypothesis tests
    """
    n_tests = len(p_values)
    adjusted_alpha = alpha / n_tests
    
    significant = p_values < adjusted_alpha
    return significant, adjusted_alpha

atoms.title: parameter sensitivity
atoms.summary: Test how sensitive results are to parameter changes

props.formula:
def parameter_sensitivity(data, strategy_class, param_name, param_range):
    """
    Test how sensitive results are to parameter changes
    """
    results = {}
    for param_value in param_range:
        strategy = strategy_class(**{param_name: param_value})
        returns = strategy.backtest(data)
        results[param_value] = calculate_sharpe(returns)
    
    # Check if results are stable across parameter range
    values = list(results.values())
    stability = np.std(values) / np.mean(values)
    
    return results, stability

atoms.title: strategy archetypes
atoms.summary: Strategy archetypes classify trading strategies by the market behavior they exploit, not by timeframe or instrument. Archetypes describe *why* a strategy has expected positive return under certain conditions.

applications: Strategy selection based on market conditions
Portfolio diversification across archetypes
Understanding strategy performance attribution
Designing hybrid approaches with clear signal hierarchy
Setting appropriate expectations for win rate and skew

atoms.title: trend following
atoms.summary: Markets exhibit persistent directional regimes driven by sustained capital flows.

props.explanation: Identify sustained directional movement Enter after trend confirmation Exit on regime break, not noise Win Rate: 30-40% (low) Skew: POSITIVE (occasional large wins) Tail Risk: MODERATE - losses are bounded by stops Drawdowns: Extended choppy periods cause bleeding Large winners offset frequent small losses Performs well in trending markets Underperforms in range-bound markets Positive skew means you profit from fat tails Moving average crossovers Donchian channel breakouts Time-series momentum Managed futures / CTA strategies
props.caution: *Should we be exposed in this direction?* Risk Warning: Trend following has LOW win rate. Do NOT expect to be right often. The edge comes from letting winners run far enough to compensate for frequent small losses.

atoms.title: momentum strategy
atoms.summary: Price movement exhibits short-term persistence due to acceleration, positioning pressure, and behavioral effects.

props.explanation: Measure rate of change or acceleration Enter during expansion of pressure Exit as momentum decays Win Rate: 50-60% (moderate) Skew: NEUTRAL to slightly positive Tail Risk: MODERATE - vulnerable to sharp reversals Drawdowns: Quick reversals can trap momentum traders Higher win rate than trend following Shorter holding periods Vulnerable to sharp reversals Works both within and outside trends RSI / ROC momentum MACD-based systems Cross-sectional momentum Short-term continuation models
props.caution: *Is directional pressure increasing or fading right now?* Relationship to Trend Following: Trend defines *regime*. Momentum defines *timing*. In practice, trend is often used as a filter and momentum as an entry/exit engine.

atoms.title: breakout strategy
atoms.summary: Periods of volatility compression are followed by expansion as new information is revealed.

props.explanation: Often marks **trend initiation** Combines momentum entry with trend potential Accepts false breakouts as cost of discovery Win Rate: 40-50% Skew: POSITIVE (breakouts that work tend to run) Tail Risk: MODERATE - false breakouts are common Drawdowns: Choppy markets produce many false signals Range breakouts Volatility squeeze breakouts (Bollinger Band squeeze) Opening range breakouts
props.caution: *Is a new move beginning?* Usage Note: Breakouts bridge momentum (entry timing) and trend (regime establishment). They work best when combined with regime filters.
applications: Trend-following entry signals
Volatility breakout strategies
Channel breakout systems
News/event trading
Swing trading entries
props.source_wording: Breakout signals identify when price moves beyond a defined range or threshold, indicating potential start of a new trend or acceleration of existing trend. They are the foundation of trend-following strategies.

atoms.title: volatility strategy
atoms.summary: Profit from significant price movements regardless of direction.

props.explanation: Trade when volatility expands Direction-agnostic (long or short based on breakout direction) Exit when volatility contracts or move exhausts Win Rate: 30-50% Skew: NEUTRAL to slightly positive Tail Risk: MODERATE - whipsaws during false breakouts Drawdowns: Choppy, range-bound markets produce losses Works in both trending and ranging markets Requires volatility to capture meaningful moves Often uses ATR, Bollinger Bands, or volatility indicators Not directionally biased ATR breakout strategies Bollinger Band squeeze breakouts Straddle/strangle equivalents in spot Keltner Channel expansions Volatility expansion trades
props.caution: *Is the market moving enough to capture profitable swings?* Usage Note: Volatility strategies don't predict direction - they trade movement size. Best in markets with alternating quiet and active periods.

atoms.title: mean reversion
atoms.summary: Prices temporarily deviate from equilibrium and revert as liquidity providers and arbitrageurs act.

props.explanation: Buy oversold conditions Sell overbought conditions Exit near perceived mean Win Rate: 60-70% (high) Skew: NEGATIVE (occasional large losses) Tail Risk: HIGH - can fail catastrophically during trend emergence Drawdowns: Single large losses can wipe out many small wins High win rate is psychologically seductive Performs best in range-bound regimes **DANGEROUS** in trending markets Negative skew means tail losses are disproportionately large RSI mean reversion Bollinger Band reversion Pairs trading Statistical arbitrage
props.caution: *Has price extended too far from fair value?* CRITICAL WARNING: DO NOT describe mean reversion as "lower risk" or "safer." High win rate does NOT equal low risk. The negative skew means losses, when they occur, are disproportionately large. Mean reversion strategies can and do blow up when trends emerge. "The trend is your friend" exists because fighting trends is dangerous.
applications: Statistical arbitrage pairs trading
RSI/Bollinger Band reversal trades
ETF premium/discount arbitrage
Cross-sectional equity strategies
Funding rate arbitrage in crypto
props.source_wording: Mean reversion is the tendency for prices to return to an average level over time. Mean reversion strategies profit by identifying temporary deviations from fair value and trading on the expectation that prices will revert.

atoms.title: signal types
atoms.summary: Signal types classify trading signals by their role in the decision-making process. Understanding signal types helps traders combine signals effectively and build robust strategies.

props.mapping_signal_types_to_archetype: | Archetype | Typical Signal Role | |-----------|---------------------| | Trend Following | **Filter** - Establishes directional context | | Momentum | **Entry / Exit** - Times entries and exits | | Mean Reversion | **Entry** - Triggers counter-trend position | | Regime Detection | **Meta-Filter** - Gates which archetypes to deploy |
props.how_signal_types_work_together: A typical strategy combines multiple signal types: def generate_trade_signal(data): """ Combine signal types for robust decision-making """ # FILTER: Is the environment right for trading? if not filter_price_above_200_sma(data): return None  # Only trade in uptrend # ENTRY: Should we get in now? if not entry_rsi_oversold(data): return None  # Wait for entry trigger # CONFIRMATION: Are we sure? if not confirmation_macd_positive(data): return None  # Need momentum confirmation return "LONG"  # All conditions met def check_exit(data, position): """ Exit signals close positions """ if position == "LONG": if exit_rsi_overbought(data): return "CLOSE" return "HOLD"
props.signal_type_characteristic: **Entry Signals:** - Fire at specific moments when trade setup is complete - Typically require immediate action - Often based on crossovers, breakouts, or pattern completions - Examples: `sma_cross_up`, `macd_bullish_cross`, `rsi_oversold` **Exit Signals:** - Indicate when to close existing positions - Can be based on profit targets, stop losses, or reversal conditions - Should be defined before trade entry - Examples: `sma_cross_down`, `macd_bearish_cross`, `rsi_overbought` **Filter Signals:** - Provide ongoing context rather than discrete triggers - Answer: "Should we be trading in this direction at all?" - Reduce false signals by ensuring market environment is favorable - Examples: `is_above_sma`, `adx_strong_trend`, `vwap_above` **Confirmation Signals:** - Add conviction to entry signals - Reduce false positives by requiring multiple conditions - Often come from different indicator categories (trend + momentum + volume) - Examples: `macd_positive`, `obv_bullish`, `bb_squeeze`

props.formula:
def statistical_entry(returns, threshold_zscore=2):
    """
    Enter on statistical deviation
    """
    zscore = (returns - returns.mean()) / returns.std()
    long_signal = zscore < -threshold_zscore
    short_signal = zscore > threshold_zscore
    return long_signal, short_signal

props.formula:
def pullback_entry(price, trend_signal, pullback_threshold=0.02):
    """
    Enter on pullback within trend
    """
    recent_high = price.rolling(20).max()
    pullback_pct = (recent_high - price) / recent_high
    
    entry = trend_signal & (pullback_pct > pullback_threshold)
    return entry

atoms.title: breakout entry
atoms.summary: Enter on breakout of recent range

props.formula:
def breakout_entry(price, period=20):
    """
    Enter on breakout of recent range
    """
    high = price.rolling(period).max()
    low = price.rolling(period).min()
    
    long_entry = price > high.shift(1)
    short_entry = price < low.shift(1)
    return long_entry, short_entry

atoms.title: fixed stop
atoms.summary: Exit on fixed percentage loss

props.formula:
def fixed_stop_exit(entry_price, current_price, stop_pct=0.02, direction='long'):
    """
    Exit on fixed percentage loss
    """
    if direction == 'long':
        stop_price = entry_price * (1 - stop_pct)
        exit_signal = current_price <= stop_price
    else:
        stop_price = entry_price * (1 + stop_pct)
        exit_signal = current_price >= stop_price
    return exit_signal, stop_price
props.explanation: Very liquid instruments with stable volatility. Short horizons where structure is unclear. High-volatility assets: frequent whipsaws. Trend days: too tight relative to ATR.
notes: When it works:
When it fails:
Toolkit: `fixed_percentage_stop`.
Limitations: Doesn't account for asset volatility or market structure.
props.source_wording: Fixed percentage stops are simple, but volatility is not constant, so this method is easy to mis-calibrate.

atoms.title: atr-based stop
atoms.summary: Exit based on ATR distance

props.formula:
def atr_stop_exit(entry_price, current_price, atr, multiplier=2.0, direction='long'):
    """
    Exit based on ATR distance
    """
    stop_distance = atr * multiplier
    if direction == 'long':
        stop_price = entry_price - stop_distance
        exit_signal = current_price <= stop_price
    else:
        stop_price = entry_price + stop_distance
        exit_signal = current_price >= stop_price
    return exit_signal, stop_price
props.explanation: 1.5 ATR: tight, more whipsaws 2.0 ATR: common default 3.0 ATR: wide, fewer whipsaws but larger losses per stop Tight: 1.5 ATR (more whipsaws, quicker exit) Standard: 2.0 ATR (balanced) Wide: 3.0 ATR (fewer whipsaws, larger losses)
notes: How to choose a multiplier:
Calibration rule: pick a multiplier that matches your timeframe and validate it with backtests.
Toolkit: `atr_stop`.
props.source_wording: ATR-based stops scale with volatility, producing more consistent behavior across assets and regimes.

def fixed_target_exit(entry_price, current_price, target_pct=0.04, direction='long'):

    if direction == 'long':
        target_price = entry_price * (1 + target_pct)
        exit_signal = current_price >= target_price
    else:

        exit_signal = current_price <= target_price

atoms.title: simple trailing stop
atoms.summary: Trail stop behind price

props.formula:
def trailing_stop(prices, trail_pct=0.02, direction='long'):
    """
    Trail stop behind price
    """
    if direction == 'long':
        highest = prices.expanding().max()
        stop = highest * (1 - trail_pct)
    else:
        lowest = prices.expanding().min()
        stop = lowest * (1 + trail_pct)
    return stop
notes: Toolkit: `percentage_trailing_stop`.
props.source_wording: Percentage trailing is simple and works best in smooth trends. It often fails in choppy conditions.

atoms.title: atr trailing stop
atoms.summary: Trail stop by ATR distance

props.formula:
def atr_trailing_stop(prices, atr, multiplier=2.5, direction='long'):
    """
    Trail stop by ATR distance
    """
    if direction == 'long':
        highest = prices.expanding().max()
        stop = highest - (atr * multiplier)
    else:
        lowest = prices.expanding().min()
        stop = lowest + (atr * multiplier)
    return stop
notes: Toolkit: `chandelier_exit`.
props.source_wording: Chandelier exits adapt to volatility by trailing from the best price by an ATR multiple.

from hmmlearn import hmm

def hmm_regime_detection(returns, n_states=2):
    """
    HMM-based regime detection
    """
    model = hmm.GaussianHMM(n_components=n_states, covariance_type="diag")
    model.fit(returns.values.reshape(-1, 1))
    
    regime = model.predict(returns.values.reshape(-1, 1))
    return regime
props.explanation: State 1: High volatility regime (stressed market) Transition probabilities indicate regime persistence
props.source_wording: State 0: Low volatility regime (calm market)

def clean_missing_data(df):
    """
    Handle missing values appropriately
    """
    # Forward fill for prices (common approach)
    df['close'] = df['close'].fillna(method='ffill')
    
    # Don't fill volume - missing volume is meaningful
    # df['volume'] remains NaN
    
    # Drop rows with critical missing data
    df = df.dropna(subset=['open', 'high', 'low', 'close'])
    
    return df

def detect_outliers(returns, threshold=5):
    """
    Identify potential data errors
    """
    zscore = (returns - returns.mean()) / returns.std()
    outliers = abs(zscore) > threshold
    return outliers

atoms.title: split adjustment
atoms.summary: Adjust historical prices for stock splits

props.formula:
def adjust_for_splits(price, splits):
    """
    Adjust historical prices for stock splits
    """
    adjusted = price.copy()
    for split_date, split_ratio in splits.items():
        adjusted.loc[:split_date] *= split_ratio
    return adjusted

atoms.title: dividend adjustment
atoms.summary: Create total return series including dividends

props.formula:
def adjust_for_dividends(price, dividends):
    """
    Create total return series including dividends
    """
    # Calculate adjustment factor
    adjustment = (price + dividends) / price
    adjusted_price = price * adjustment.cumprod()
    return adjusted_price

atoms.title: survivorship bias prevention
atoms.summary: Include stocks that existed on date, even if later delisted

props.formula:
def include_delisted(universe, date):
    """
    Include stocks that existed on date, even if later delisted
    """
    # Point-in-time universe
    available_stocks = universe[universe['listing_date'] <= date]
    available_stocks = available_stocks[
        (available_stocks['delisting_date'].isna()) | 
        (available_stocks['delisting_date'] > date)
    ]
    return available_stocks

atoms.title: look-ahead bias prevention
atoms.summary: Return only data available on target_date

props.formula:
def point_in_time_data(df, target_date):
    """
    Return only data available on target_date
    """
    # Shift data to simulate reporting lag
    reporting_lag = pd.Timedelta(days=1)  # Or appropriate lag
    available_data = df[df.index <= target_date - reporting_lag]
    return available_data

atoms.title: core principles
atoms.summary: Things that are true of this market whether or not anyone acts on them. A strategy does not get to disagree with one: it either accounts for it or pays for it.

atoms.title: best practices
atoms.summary: Things we follow because someone has already paid to learn them. Each is a default rather than a rule -- departing from one is often right, but it should be a decision with a reason.

atoms.title: risk dimension
atoms.summary: One of the separate ways a strategy can lose money, each measured differently and none of them a substitute for the others.

comparison: Dimension · Definition · What It Measures · Common Mistake
Per-Trade Risk · Capital at risk on a single trade · Position size, stop loss distance · Confusing small stops with low risk
Strategy Skew · Shape of the return distribution · Positive (trend) vs. negative (MR) · Assuming high win rate = low risk
Regime Risk · Mismatch between strategy and market · Strategy applied to wrong conditions · Not adapting to changing markets
Drawdown Risk · Maximum capital decline · Peak-to-trough loss, recovery time · Ignoring time-in-drawdown
Tail Risk · Extreme loss probability · VaR, Expected Shortfall · Underestimating "black swan" events
Correlation Risk · Positions moving together · Portfolio-level diversification · "Diversification" failing in crisis
Liquidity Risk · Ability to exit positions · Slippage, market impact · Assuming orderly exits in stress
props.explanation: The chapter opens here because controlling one dimension reads as controlling risk: a tight stop bounds [[Per-Trade Risk]] and leaves [[Strategy Skew]] and [[Regime Risk]] exactly where they were. Seven are named -- per-trade, skew, regime, drawdown, tail, correlation and liquidity -- and the common mistake against each is the false confidence that comes from having addressed a different one.

atoms.title: per-trade risk vs. strategy risk
atoms.summary: Common Misconception: "I use tight stops, so my strategy is low risk."

props.explanation: Mean reversion with 0.5% per-trade risk still has negative skew Many small losses can accumulate into large drawdown A regime change can cause all positions to fail simultaneously
comparison: Control · What It Does · What It Does NOT Do
Tight stop loss · Limits loss on single trade · Does not change skew or regime risk
Small position size · Reduces dollar loss per trade · Does not prevent strategy blow-up
Diversification · Reduces single-asset risk · Fails when correlations spike
notes: Reality: Per-trade risk controls (position sizing, stop losses) do NOT change strategy-level risk.

atoms.title: strategy risk assessment
atoms.summary: Before deploying any strategy, answer these questions:

notes: 1. What is the skew? Positive (trend) or Negative (MR/carry)?
2. What regime does it require? Trending, ranging, or low volatility?
3. What causes it to blow up? Trend emergence? Volatility spike? Correlation breakdown?
4. How long can drawdowns last? Weeks? Months? Years?
5. What is the maximum historical drawdown? Can you survive it?
6. How correlated are the positions? Is diversification real or illusory?
When evaluating or building a strategy:
1. Classify the archetype - Trend following, momentum, mean reversion, carry, event-driven
2. Identify the skew - Will wins or losses be larger on average?
3. Define the failure mode - Under what conditions does this strategy fail catastrophically?
4. Size for the tail - Position size assuming the worst-case scenario happens
5. Monitor regime fit - Continuously assess if market conditions suit the strategy
props.caution: The First Rule of Risk: Preserve capital. You cannot recover from total loss.

atoms.title: per-trade risk
atoms.summary: Capital at risk on a single trade. Position size, stop loss distance. Confusing small stops with low risk

atoms.title: strategy skew
atoms.summary: Shape of the return distribution. Positive (trend) vs. negative (MR). Assuming high win rate = low risk

atoms.title: regime risk
atoms.summary: Mismatch between strategy and market. Strategy applied to wrong conditions. Not adapting to changing markets

atoms.title: drawdown risk
atoms.summary: Maximum capital decline. Peak-to-trough loss, recovery time. Ignoring time-in-drawdown

atoms.title: tail risk
atoms.summary: Extreme loss probability. VaR, Expected Shortfall. Underestimating "black swan" events

atoms.title: correlation risk
atoms.summary: Positions moving together. Portfolio-level diversification. "Diversification" failing in crisis

atoms.title: liquidity risk
atoms.summary: Ability to exit positions. Slippage, market impact. Assuming orderly exits in stress

atoms.title: trading rules
atoms.summary: Trading rules and protocols are predefined guidelines that govern trading behavior, risk limits, and decision-making processes. These rules establish boundaries that protect capital, enforce discipline, and remove emotional decision-making from trading operations.

props.implementation_framework: Implementation should behave like a pre-trade checklist with hard stops. How to operationalize: - Convert each rule into a measurable threshold (percent of equity, counts, ratios). - Run the checks before opening a trade, not after. - Treat violations as automatic "no trade" outcomes. - Review and adjust thresholds on a schedule (monthly/quarterly), not during a drawdown. Common failure modes: - Risk is computed using a stop you would not actually execute. - Multiple small, correlated positions create one big bet. - "Make it back" sizing after losses (breaks survival math). Toolkit: `TradingRules`, `check_trading_rules`, `daily_loss_limit_status` in `MangroveAI.utils.risk_management_toolkit`.

atoms.title: max risk per trade
atoms.summary: Amount willing to lose on a single trade. 1% of account

props.description: Amount willing to lose on a single trade

atoms.title: max daily loss
atoms.summary: Daily drawdown limit before stopping trading. 5% of account

props.description: Daily drawdown limit before stopping trading

atoms.title: max weekly loss
atoms.summary: Weekly drawdown limit before break/cooldown. 10% of account

atoms.title: max open trades
atoms.summary: Maximum simultaneous positions. 25 positions

atoms.title: reward-to-risk ratio
atoms.summary: Risk-reward ratio (R:R) compares the potential profit of a trade to its potential loss. It is a fundamental metric for evaluating trade quality and setting realistic expectations.

props.description: Minimum acceptable R:R for any setup
notes: Minimum acceptable R:R for any setup. >= 2:1
Risk-reward is only meaningful if the stop is real and the target is realistic.
Checklist:
Toolkit: `risk_reward_ratio`.
props.explanation: Stop is placed at invalidation (not a random percent). Target is based on structure (not hope). If computed risk is non-positive, the setup is invalid.

atoms.title: position sizing
atoms.summary: Position sizing determines the amount of capital to allocate to each trade based on risk parameters, account size, and strategy characteristics. Proper position sizing balances potential returns against risk of ruin. The goal is to keep risk constant across trades regardless of entry price or volatility.

props.default_value: (Account Balance x max risk) / (entry price - stop loss)
notes: Contracts per trade. (Account Balance x max risk) / (entry price - stop loss)
applications: Determining number of shares/contracts per trade
Normalizing risk across different asset volatilities
Managing overall portfolio exposure
Scaling positions based on conviction
Adapting to changing market conditions

atoms.title: cool down period
atoms.summary: Time to stop trading after hitting daily loss. Remainder of the day

props.description: Time to stop trading after hitting daily loss

atoms.title: trading hours
atoms.summary: Allowed trading window. 8:00 AM - 11:30 AM

atoms.title: profit lock rule
atoms.summary: Stop trading after hitting daily goal. 1%-2% gain (competition: >5%)

props.description: Stop trading after hitting daily goal

atoms.title: fixed fractional position sizing
atoms.summary: Risk a fixed percentage of capital on each trade.

props.explanation: Account: $100,000 Risk per trade: 1% ($1,000) Entry: $50, Stop: $48 Risk per share: $2 Position size: $1,000 / $2 = 500 shares Conservative: 0.5% per trade Moderate: 1% per trade Aggressive: 2% per trade Maximum: 5% per trade (very risky)
notes: Position Size = floor((Account Value x Risk Fraction) / abs(Entry Price - Stop Price))
Implementation note: See `MangroveAI.utils.risk_management_toolkit.position_size_fixed_fractional`.

atoms.title: volatility-adjusted position sizing
atoms.summary: Size positions inversely to asset volatility for equal risk contribution.

notes: Position Value = (Account Value x Target Volatility) / Asset Volatility
Position Size = floor(Position Value / Asset Price)
Implementation note: See `MangroveAI.utils.risk_management_toolkit.position_size_volatility_target`.
Risk per Unit = ATR x ATR Multiplier
Position Size = floor((Account Value x Risk Fraction) / Risk per Unit)
Implementation note: See `MangroveAI.utils.risk_management_toolkit.position_size_atr`.

atoms.title: kelly criterion
atoms.summary: Mathematically optimal bet size to maximize long-term growth.

notes: Kelly Fraction = W - (1 - W) / R
Where:
W = Win rate (probability of winning, 0-1)
R = Win/Loss ratio (average win / average loss)
Implementation note: See `MangroveAI.utils.risk_management_toolkit.kelly_fraction` and `MangroveAI.utils.risk_management_toolkit.fractional_kelly_fraction`.
Caution: Full Kelly is very aggressive. Most practitioners use Half-Kelly or Quarter-Kelly.

atoms.title: position size
atoms.summary: The fundamental position sizing formula ensures consistent risk across all trades:

props.explanation: Account Balance: $50,000 Risk per Trade: 1% ($500) Entry Price: $100 Stop Loss: $95 Risk per Share: $5 Position Size: $500 / $5 = 100 shares
notes: Position Size = (Account Balance x Risk per Trade) / abs(Entry Price - Stop Loss)
Implementation note: See `MangroveAI.utils.risk_management_toolkit.position_size_fixed_fractional`.
This formula normalizes risk regardless of the stock price or stop distance, ensuring each trade risks the same percentage of capital.

atoms.title: drawdown controls
atoms.summary: Drawdown controls are mechanisms to limit cumulative losses during adverse periods, protecting capital and allowing recovery. They trigger protective actions when losses exceed predefined thresholds.

applications: Daily loss limits for day traders
Strategy-level drawdown stops
Portfolio-level risk budgets
Position reduction during adverse periods
Trading suspension triggers

atoms.title: recovery mathematics
atoms.summary: Implication: Avoiding large drawdowns is more important than maximizing returns.

comparison: Drawdown · Required Recovery

atoms.title: maximum drawdown limits
atoms.summary: Maximum drawdown limits are portfolio-level circuit breakers. They are not predictions; they are safety rails.

props.explanation: Set a hard drawdown limit that halts trading (e.g., 20%). Add a warning level that forces size reduction (e.g., 10% if the limit is 20%). Decide resumption rules in advance (time-based cooldown, or performance-based reset).
notes: Practical guidance:
Toolkit: `max_drawdown_action`.

atoms.title: progressive drawdown response
atoms.summary: A progressive response reduces exposure as losses accumulate, which helps avoid keeping full size during your worst regime.

props.explanation: 0-5% drawdown: normal 5-10%: caution (reduce size modestly) 10-15%: reduce (cut size materially) 15-20%: minimal (only highest quality trades) >20%: stop
notes: One simple ladder:
Toolkit: `progressive_drawdown_response`.

atoms.title: daily loss limits
atoms.summary: Daily loss limits protect you from both streaks and emotional decision-making after losses.

props.explanation: Use a clear threshold in dollars or percent of equity (or both). Include a warning band (e.g., 80% of the limit) that forces reduced size. When the limit is hit, stop trading for the rest of the day.
notes: Implementation principles:
Toolkit: `daily_loss_limit_status`.

atoms.title: time-based drawdown recovery
atoms.summary: Drawdown depth is only half the story. Time-in-drawdown matters because strategies can be statistically viable but psychologically impossible to follow.

props.explanation: Frequency: how often you exceed a threshold. Duration: how long you remain above it. Trend: whether recovery time is increasing over months (possible regime change).
notes: Track:
Toolkit: `drawdown_recovery_stats`.

atoms.title: stop-loss and take-profit engineering
atoms.summary: Stop-loss (SL) and take-profit (TP) orders are predetermined exit points that define risk and reward for each trade. A stop-loss caps potential losses by automatically closing a position when price moves against you, while a take-profit locks in gains by closing when price reaches a target level. Well-engineered SL/TP levels balance protecting capital against allowing normal price fluctuations.

props.stop_placement_guideline: **Where NOT to Place Stops:** - Exactly at round numbers (obvious to everyone) - Exactly at obvious support/resistance (liquidity targets) - Too tight (normal volatility triggers) - Too wide (defeats purpose of risk management) **Where to Place Stops:** - Below significant swing lows (for longs) - Above significant swing highs (for shorts) - Beyond ATR-defined volatility range - At levels that invalidate trade thesis ---
props.stop_loss_placement_guideline: | Position | Stop Placement | |----------|----------------| | Long | Below support level or swing low | | Short | Above resistance level or swing high | | Volatility-Adjusted | Entry minus (ATR x 1.5 to 2.0) | **Where NOT to Place Stops:** - Exactly at round numbers (obvious to all) - Exactly at obvious support/resistance (liquidity targets) - Too tight (normal volatility triggers) - Too wide (defeats risk management purpose) ---

atoms.title: structure-based stop
atoms.summary: Structure-based stops place the stop where the trade thesis is invalidated (e.g., below the swing low for a long).

props.explanation: Use obvious invalidation points (prior swing, range boundary, key level). Add a buffer (often ATR-based) to reduce stop hunts. If the stop is too far, reduce size or skip the trade; do not widen risk beyond plan.
notes: Guidelines:
Toolkit: `structure_stop`.

atoms.title: break-even stop
atoms.summary: Break-even stops reduce downside after the trade has proven itself, but they also increase the chance of getting stopped out before the real move.

props.explanation: Trigger on profit fraction (e.g., +0.5% to +1%) or on an R multiple (e.g., 1R). Avoid moving to break-even too early in volatile markets.
notes: Use a trigger:
Toolkit: `break_even_stop`.

atoms.title: parabolic sar-based
atoms.summary: Parabolic SAR is a momentum-based trailing mechanism. It tends to flip quickly in sideways markets.

notes: Toolkit: `parabolic_sar_stop`.

atoms.title: partial exits / scale-out
atoms.summary: Scale-outs balance realized gains with participation in extended moves. A typical plan is 1.5R / 2R / 3R targets with a runner.

props.explanation: Define target fractions ahead of time (e.g., 33% / 33% / 34%). Move stops only according to plan (break-even after 1R, trail after 1.5R, etc.).
notes: Risk controls:
Toolkit: `scale_out_targets`.

atoms.title: trailing behavior after targets
atoms.summary: Move stop to break-even after 1R

props.explanation: Trail stop to lock in 1R after 1.5R Trail stop to lock in 1.5R after 2R Let runner ride with trailing stop

atoms.title: portfolio risk
atoms.summary: Portfolio risk management addresses the aggregate risk of multiple positions, considering correlations, concentration, and the interaction effects between positions.

atoms.title: correlation-adjusted position sizing
atoms.summary: Correlation-adjusted sizing prevents accidental concentration. When assets are highly correlated, "diversification" is an illusion.

props.explanation: Compute covariance from recent returns. Estimate portfolio volatility under target weights. Scale weights down if volatility exceeds your budget.
notes: Practical approach:
Toolkit: `correlation_adjusted_weights`, `portfolio_volatility_from_covariance`.

atoms.title: concentration limits
atoms.summary: Concentration limits cap the damage from a single bad thesis.

props.explanation: Single position: 5-10% of portfolio Sector: 20-30% of portfolio Asset class: 40-60% of portfolio Correlated cluster: 15-25% of portfolio
notes: Toolkit: `check_concentration_limits`.

atoms.title: value at risk (var)
atoms.summary: Maximum expected loss over a time period at a confidence level.

props.explanation: VaR ignores the severity beyond the threshold (tail risk). VaR depends heavily on the chosen window and regime.
notes: VaR is a quantile of the loss distribution. It is a communication and budgeting tool, not a guarantee.
Key caveats:
Toolkit: `value_at_risk_historical`.
Interpretation: 95% VaR of 2% means there's a 5% chance of losing more than 2% on any given day.

atoms.title: expected shortfall (cvar)
atoms.summary: Expected loss given that loss exceeds VaR (average of worst cases).

notes: Expected Shortfall (CVaR) estimates the average loss in the worst tail and is generally more informative than VaR for risk control.
Toolkit: `expected_shortfall_historical`.
Use: More informative than VaR for tail risk assessment.

atoms.title: portfolio beta and market exposure
atoms.summary: Portfolio beta estimates sensitivity to a broad market factor. It helps answer: "If the market drops 1%, how much should I expect to lose?"

props.explanation: Compute beta over multiple windows (short and medium term). Treat beta as a moving estimate, not a constant.
notes: Good practice:
Toolkit: `portfolio_beta`.

atoms.title: capital efficiency
atoms.summary: Capital efficiency measures how effectively capital is deployed to generate returns, balancing the use of leverage, margin, and buying power against risk.

atoms.title: capital allocation framework
atoms.summary: Capital allocation should separate "risk budget" from "capital budget." The same dollar allocation can produce very different risk.

props.explanation: Reserve a cash buffer (for margin calls, volatility spikes, opportunities). Define allocation weights per strategy and review periodically. Avoid reallocating reactively based on short-term performance.
notes: Guidelines:
Toolkit: `allocate_capital`.

atoms.title: leverage management
atoms.summary: Leverage is exposure relative to equity. It amplifies both returns and drawdowns.

props.explanation: Gross leverage (sum of absolute exposures / equity) Net leverage (net exposure / equity) Long/short balance (for hedged books) Conservative: 1x gross Moderate: 2x gross Aggressive: 3-4x gross Maximum institutional: 6-8x gross (hedge funds)
notes: Monitor:
Toolkit: `effective_leverage`.

atoms.title: capital utilization metrics
atoms.summary: Capital utilization matters because deploying capital without a risk budget is a common failure mode.

props.explanation: Utilization = capital deployed / max capital Return on deployed capital (annualized) Return on max capital (return on deployed x utilization) Efficiency ratio (return on deployed / utilization)
notes: Simple metrics:
Toolkit: `capital_efficiency_metrics`.

atoms.title: break-even win rate
atoms.summary: Break-even Win Rate = 1 / (1 + R:R)

comparison: R:R Ratio · Break-Even Win Rate
notes: Toolkit: `breakeven_win_rate`.

atoms.title: expectancy
atoms.summary: Expected return per dollar risked.

props.explanation: Expectancy = (Win Rate x Avg Win) - ((1 - Win Rate) x Avg Loss)
notes: Expectancy summarizes your edge:
Toolkit: `expectancy`.
Use R-multiples to compare strategies across assets and timeframes.
Toolkit: `r_multiple_expectancy`.

atoms.title: setting realistic targets
atoms.summary: Targets should be achievable given volatility and nearby structure.

props.explanation: Target distance in ATR multiples (very large multiples are rarely hit). Obstacles between entry and target (major levels, ranges, pivots). If the target requires a market regime change, it is not a target, it is a dream.
notes: Sanity checks:
Toolkit: `evaluate_target_realism` is not implemented in the toolkit; treat this as a framework to build per-strategy.

atoms.title: risk of ruin
atoms.summary: Risk of ruin is the probability of losing a specified percentage of capital (often defined as 50% or total loss) based on position sizing and strategy characteristics. It quantifies the survivability of a trading approach.

atoms.title: risk of ruin formula
atoms.summary: Risk of ruin depends primarily on edge and risk-per-trade. Small increases in risk-per-trade can massively increase ruin probability.

notes: Toolkit: `risk_of_ruin_classic`.

atoms.title: monte carlo ruin estimation
atoms.summary: Monte Carlo simulation helps model streaks and compounding. Use conservative assumptions.

notes: Toolkit: `monte_carlo_ruin`.

atoms.title: reducing risk of ruin
atoms.summary: Treat risk-per-trade as the main dial:

props.explanation: Reduce risk-per-trade during drawdowns. Use fraction-of-Kelly as a ceiling, not a target. Prefer robustness over theoretical optimality.
notes: Toolkit: `safe_risk_fraction_for_target_ruin`, `fractional_kelly_fraction`.

atoms.title: scenario analysis
atoms.summary: Scenario analysis evaluates portfolio performance under specific hypothetical market conditions, including historical stress events and constructed worst-case scenarios.

atoms.title: historical stress tests
atoms.summary: Historical stress tests approximate: "What would have happened if we lived through that again?"

props.explanation: Stress tests are scenarios, not forecasts. Include correlation spikes (diversification breaks in crises).
notes: Important:
Toolkit: `historical_stress_test`.

atoms.title: hypothetical scenario construction
atoms.summary: Hypothetical scenarios let you test combinations you have not experienced in the data.

props.explanation: Start from a base scenario and apply adjustments (worse equities, worse bonds, vol shock). Include a liquidity shock (wider spreads, bigger gaps) in operational planning.
notes: Approach:
Toolkit: `construct_scenario`.

atoms.title: correlation stress testing
atoms.summary: Correlation stress testing asks: "What if correlations move toward 1?" This is often the real risk in diversified portfolios.

props.explanation: Compute volatility under normal covariance. Replace covariance/correlation with a stressed version and recompute. Compare the increase; size down if the stressed case is unacceptable.
notes: Practical steps:
Toolkit: `correlation_adjusted_weights`, `portfolio_volatility_from_covariance`.

atoms.title: tail risk analysis
atoms.summary: Tail risk analysis focuses on the worst outcomes rather than the average.

props.explanation: Left tail mean and worst loss (bad days) Right tail mean and best gain (good days) Tail ratio (are good tails large enough to justify bad tails?)
notes: What to watch:
Toolkit: `tail_risk_analysis`.

atoms.title: scenario action plans
atoms.summary: Scenario action plans turn risk metrics into behavior so you are not improvising under stress.

props.explanation: Severe scenario: cut risk in half, remove leverage, raise cash Moderate: reduce size, tighten risk controls, add hedges Mild: monitor and review exposures
notes: Example actions:
Toolkit: `scenario_response_plan`.

atoms.title: core principles
atoms.summary: Things that are true of this market whether or not anyone acts on them. A strategy does not get to disagree with one: it either accounts for it or pays for it.

atoms.title: best practices
atoms.summary: Things we follow because someone has already paid to learn them. Each is a default rather than a rule -- departing from one is often right, but it should be a decision with a reason.

atoms.title: trend indicators
atoms.summary: Trend indicators are mathematical calculations applied to price data to identify the direction and strength of market trends. They smooth price action to filter noise and reveal underlying directional bias, helping traders align with prevailing market momentum. **Core Principles:** - **Lag vs. Smoothing Trade-off**: More smoothing means more lag but cleaner signals - **Trend Confirmation**: Indicators confirm trend direction, not predict reversals - **Multiple Timeframe Agreement**: Trend indicators across timeframes should align - **Trend Following**: Best used in trending markets, not ranges - **Price Always Leads**: Indicators are derivatives of price; price changes first **Common Use Cases:** - Identifying trend direction for trade bias - Dynamic support/resistance levels - Entry triggers on pullbacks to moving averages - Exit signals when trend indicators turn - Filtering out counter-trend trades ---

atoms.title: parabolic sar
atoms.summary: Stop and Reverse system that provides potential entry/exit points by plotting dots above or below price, indicating trend direction and potential reversal points.

props.formula:
SAR_tomorrow = SAR_today + AF * (EP - SAR_today)

Where:
  AF = Acceleration Factor (starts at 0.02, increments by 0.02, max 0.20)
  EP = Extreme Point (highest high in uptrend, lowest low in downtrend)
props.interpretation: - Dots below price: Uptrend (long) - Dots above price: Downtrend (short) - Dot flip signals potential trend reversal
props.applications: - Trailing stop-loss placement - Trend direction confirmation - Entry signals when dots flip - Best in trending markets; poor in ranges (whipsaws)

atoms.title: standard deviation
atoms.summary: Statistical measure of the dispersion of returns around the mean.

props.formula:
Variance = Sum((x_i - mean)^2) / (n-1)
Standard Deviation = sqrt(Variance)

Annualized Vol = Daily Std Dev * sqrt(252)
props.interpretation: - Higher std dev: More volatile - Lower std dev: Less volatile - Used to normalize comparisons across assets ---

atoms.title: volatility index
atoms.summary: Market expectation of near-term volatility implied by S&P 500 index option prices.

props.interpretation: - VIX < 15: Low volatility / complacency - VIX 15-20: Normal volatility - VIX 20-30: Elevated volatility / uncertainty - VIX > 30: High volatility / fear - VIX spikes often coincide with market bottoms
props.applications: - Market sentiment gauge - Regime classification - Volatility trading strategies - Portfolio hedging timing ---

atoms.title: market breadth
atoms.summary: Market breadth indicators measure the participation and health of the overall market by analyzing the number of advancing vs. declining stocks, new highs/lows, and other internal market metrics.

atoms.title: advance-decline line
atoms.summary: Cumulative measure of the difference between advancing and declining stocks.

props.formula:
Daily A/D = Advancing Stocks - Declining Stocks
A/D Line = Cumulative sum of Daily A/D
props.interpretation: - Rising A/D Line: Broad participation, healthy market - Falling A/D Line: Narrow participation, weak market - A/D divergence from index: Warning signal - A/D making new highs with index: Confirms strength ---

atoms.title: mcclellan oscillator
atoms.summary: Market breadth oscillator based on the difference between 19-day and 39-day EMAs of daily advance-decline data.

props.formula: McClellan Oscillator = EMA(A-D, 19) - EMA(A-D, 39)
props.interpretation: - Oscillator > 0: Bullish breadth - Oscillator < 0: Bearish breadth - Extreme positive readings: Overbought - Extreme negative readings: Oversold - Divergences with price signal potential reversals ---

atoms.title: mcclellan summation index
atoms.summary: Cumulative sum of the McClellan Oscillator, providing a longer-term view of market breadth.

props.formula: Summation Index = Cumulative sum of McClellan Oscillator
props.interpretation: - Rising Summation Index: Bull market environment - Falling Summation Index: Bear market environment - Extreme readings indicate potential reversals ---

atoms.title: arms index
atoms.summary: Measures the relationship between advancing/declining stocks and advancing/declining volume.

props.formula: TRIN = (Advancing Issues / Declining Issues) / (Advancing Volume / Declining Volume)
props.interpretation: - TRIN < 1: Bullish (more volume in advancers) - TRIN > 1: Bearish (more volume in decliners) - TRIN < 0.5: Extremely bullish - TRIN > 2.0: Extremely bearish (often contrarian buy signal) ---

atoms.title: hidden divergence
atoms.summary: Bullish Hidden: Price makes higher low, oscillator makes lower low (trend continuation)

props.explanation: Bearish Hidden: Price makes lower high, oscillator makes higher high (trend continuation)

atoms.title: failure swings
atoms.summary: Bullish Failure Swing: Oscillator fails to reach previous low, then breaks above intervening high

props.explanation: Bearish Failure Swing: Oscillator fails to reach previous high, then breaks below intervening low

atoms.title: oscillator trend lines
atoms.summary: Draw trend lines on oscillator, not just price

props.explanation: Oscillator trend line breaks can precede price breaks

atoms.title: range shift
atoms.summary: In uptrends: RSI tends to oscillate 40-80 instead of 30-70

props.explanation: In downtrends: RSI tends to oscillate 20-60 instead of 30-70 Adjust overbought/oversold thresholds based on trend

atoms.title: variable index dynamic average (vidya)
atoms.summary: Volatility-adjusted smoothing

props.explanation: More responsive during high volatility

atoms.title: return indicators
atoms.summary: Return indicators measure price changes over time, providing metrics for momentum, performance, and risk-adjusted returns. Unlike oscillators that normalize values, return indicators show actual percentage or absolute changes.

atoms.title: core principles
atoms.summary: Things that are true of this market whether or not anyone acts on them. A strategy does not get to disagree with one: it either accounts for it or pays for it.

atoms.title: best practices
atoms.summary: Things we follow because someone has already paid to learn them. Each is a default rather than a rule -- departing from one is often right, but it should be a decision with a reason.

atoms.title: multi-bar patterns
atoms.summary: Multi-bar patterns are price formations spanning multiple candlesticks that reveal consolidation, momentum shifts, and potential breakout setups beyond traditional candlestick patterns.

atoms.title: pin bar
atoms.summary: A bar with a long wick (tail) representing rejection of a price level, with a small body opposite the wick.

props.explanation: Long lower wick (2x+ body) Small body in upper portion Close above midpoint of range Found at support Long upper wick (2x+ body) Small body in lower portion Close below midpoint of range Found at resistance Entry: Break of pin bar in direction of signal Stop: Beyond the wick High probability at key levels with trend

atoms.title: two-bar reversal
atoms.summary: Two consecutive bars forming a reversal pattern at an extreme.

props.explanation: First bar: Strong bearish close (close in lower portion of range) Second bar: Strong bullish close (close in upper portion of range), closes above first bar's open Combined forms a hammer-like structure The `close_proximity` parameter (default 0.25) controls how close the close must be to the extreme -- 0.25 means within 25% of the bar's range First bar: Strong bullish close (close in upper portion of range) Second bar: Strong bearish close (close in lower portion of range), closes below first bar's open Combined forms a shooting star-like structure

atoms.title: head and shoulders
atoms.summary: Three peaks with the middle one highest, their intervening lows forming a neckline the pattern completes by closing below.

props.formula:
Head > Left_Shoulder > Neckline
Head > Right_Shoulder > Neckline
Right_Shoulder approximately equals Left_Shoulder height
Both shoulders retrace to approximately same neckline level
props.explanation: A distribution pattern: the failure of the third rally to reach the second is the tell, and the neckline is where that reading is confirmed or refuted. The measured move -- head to neckline, projected down from the break -- is the target the chapter gives it.
notes: Interpretation: Distribution pattern; bearish reversal after uptrend.

Head: Higher rally and decline to similar level (neckline) Right Shoulder: Lower rally and decline Neckline: Connect the lows after each shoulder Entry: Break below neckline Stop: Above right shoulder Target: Measured move (head to neckline distance projected down)
props.source_wording: Left Shoulder: Rally and decline

atoms.title: inverse head and shoulders
atoms.summary: The same three-trough shape inverted, completing on a close above the neckline that joins its intervening highs.

props.explanation: Accumulation rather than distribution, and read the same way: the third decline failing to reach the second is what makes it a base rather than a pause.
notes: Interpretation: Accumulation pattern; bullish reversal after downtrend.

Left Shoulder: Decline and rally Head: Lower decline and rally Right Shoulder: Higher decline and rally Neckline: Connect the highs Entry: Break above neckline Stop: Below right shoulder Target: Measured move (head to neckline distance projected up)
props.source_wording: Mirror image of head and shoulders.

atoms.title: double top / double bottom
atoms.summary: Two tests of nearly the same level with a retracement between them, completing on a close beyond that retracement.

props.formula:
Double_Top:
  |High_Peak1 - High_Peak2| < threshold
  Valley_Low < both Peak_Highs
  Confirmation: Close below Valley_Low

atoms.title: pattern context
atoms.summary: Pattern context refers to the market conditions and technical environment that must be present for a pattern to be valid and tradeable. Context determines whether a pattern is high probability or should be avoided.

props.contextual_requirements_by_pattern_type: **Reversal Patterns (Head & Shoulders, Double Top/Bottom, etc.):** - MUST appear after established trend - MUST be at significant support/resistance level - SHOULD have increasing volume on reversal - SHOULD align with higher timeframe levels - AVOID in middle of trend with no prior structure **Continuation Patterns (Flags, Pennants, Triangles):** - MUST appear within established trend - MUST be preceded by impulse move - SHOULD show decreasing volume during formation - SHOULD break in trend direction - AVOID if pattern is larger than preceding move **Candlestick Reversal Patterns:** - MUST be at support (bullish) or resistance (bearish) - MUST be at extreme of move (not middle) - SHOULD have prior trend to reverse - SHOULD be confirmed by next candle - AVOID isolated patterns in middle of range ---
props.location_based_context: **At Support:** - Bullish reversal patterns are valid - Bearish patterns are counter-contextual - Failed breaks below support are bullish **At Resistance:** - Bearish reversal patterns are valid - Bullish patterns are counter-contextual - Failed breaks above resistance are bearish **In No Man's Land (Middle of Range):** - Most patterns have reduced reliability - Wait for price to reach extremes - Continuation patterns require clear prior trend ---
props.timeframe_context: **Higher Timeframe Bullish:** - Trade bullish patterns on lower timeframe - Be cautious with bearish patterns - Expect pullbacks to find support **Higher Timeframe Bearish:** - Trade bearish patterns on lower timeframe - Be cautious with bullish patterns - Expect rallies to find resistance **Higher Timeframe Ranging:** - Trade both directions at range extremes - Expect failed breakouts - Reduce position size ---

atoms.title: pattern completion
atoms.summary: Pattern completion criteria are the specific conditions that must be met for a pattern to be considered complete and tradeable. Premature trading of incomplete patterns is a common source of losses.

props.completion_criteria_by_pattern: **Head and Shoulders:** - Completion: Close below neckline - Confirmation: Volume increase on break - Aggressive: Break of neckline intrabar - Conservative: Close below neckline AND follow-through **Double Top/Bottom:** - Completion: Close beyond neckline (valley/peak) - Confirmation: Retest of neckline holds - Minimum depth: At least 10% from peak to valley **Triangles:** - Completion: Close beyond triangle boundary - Timing: Preferably in last third of triangle (before apex) - Volume: Expansion on breakout - Note: Breakout within 2/3 of pattern length is ideal **Flags/Pennants:** - Completion: Break beyond flag/pennant boundary - Volume: Decrease during flag, increase on break - Time: Flag should be brief (5-15 bars typically) **Cup and Handle:** - Completion: Break above cup rim / handle high - Handle depth: Less than 50% of cup depth - Cup shape: U-shaped, not V-shaped ---

atoms.title: statistical testing for seasonality
atoms.summary: Compares returns inside a calendar period against returns outside it, and reports whether the difference could be chance.

props.formula:
from scipy import stats

def test_seasonal_effect(returns, is_seasonal):
    seasonal_returns = returns[is_seasonal]
    non_seasonal_returns = returns[~is_seasonal]
    
    t_stat, p_value = stats.ttest_ind(seasonal_returns, non_seasonal_returns)
    
    return {
        'seasonal_mean': seasonal_returns.mean(),
        'non_seasonal_mean': non_seasonal_returns.mean(),
        't_statistic': t_stat,
        'p_value': p_value,
        'significant': p_value < 0.05
    }
props.explanation: A two-sample t-test, which is what separates a seasonal effect from a story about one. The chapter is explicit that well-published effects decay, so the test is worth rerunning rather than citing.

atoms.title: volatility clustering

This creates persistence in volatility that can be modeled and exploited.

applications: Volatility forecasting for risk management

atoms.title: garch family models
atoms.summary: Models tomorrow's variance as a weighted sum of a long-run level, the most recent shock, and today's variance.

props.formula:
sigma_t^2 = omega + alpha * epsilon_(t-1)^2 + beta * sigma_(t-1)^2
from arch import arch_model

# Fit GARCH(1,1)
model = arch_model(returns, vol='Garch', p=1, q=1)
results = model.fit()

# Forecast volatility
forecast = results.forecast(horizon=5)
predicted_vol = np.sqrt(forecast.variance.values[-1])
props.explanation: The two weights are the whole model: how hard a shock hits, and how slowly it decays. Their sum approaching one is persistence -- which is [[Volatility Clustering]] measured rather than observed -- and must stay below one for the process to have a long-run level at all.
notes: Key Insight: alpha + beta close to 1 means high persistence (volatility shocks take long to decay).

sigma_t^2 = Conditional variance at time t omega = Long-run variance weight alpha = Reaction to recent shock (typically 0.05-0.15) beta = Persistence parameter (typically 0.80-0.95) alpha + beta < 1 for stationarity

atoms.title: egarch
atoms.summary: The same model on the logarithm of variance, with a term that lets a fall move volatility differently from a rise.

props.formula: log(sigma_t^2) = omega + alpha * (|z_(t-1)| - E|z|) + gamma * z_(t-1) + beta * log(sigma_(t-1)^2)
props.source_wording: Key Feature: Captures asymmetry - gamma parameter allows negative returns to impact volatility differently than positive returns (leverage effect).
props.explanation: The asymmetry is the point: the leverage effect is real and symmetric GARCH cannot express it. Working in logs also removes the need to constrain the parameters positive.

Z-Score = (Price - Moving_Average) / Standard_Deviation
def calculate_zscore(series, window=20):
    mean = series.rolling(window).mean()
    std = series.rolling(window).std()
    zscore = (series - mean) / std
    return zscore

def mean_reversion_signals(zscore, entry_threshold=2, exit_threshold=0):
    signals = pd.Series(0, index=zscore.index)
    signals[zscore < -entry_threshold] = 1  # Long
    signals[zscore > entry_threshold] = -1  # Short
    signals[abs(zscore) < exit_threshold] = 0  # Exit
    return signals
props.explanation: Z < -2: Oversold, potential long Z > +2: Overbought, potential short Z crosses 0: Exit signal

def test_cointegration(series1, series2):

    return pvalue < 0.05  # Cointegrated if p-value < 0.05
from statsmodels.regression.linear_model import OLS

# Find hedge ratio

atoms.title: bollinger band mean reversion
atoms.summary: Buys below the lower band and sells above the upper, closing as price returns to the middle.

props.formula:
def bollinger_mean_reversion(close, window=20, num_std=2):
    middle = close.rolling(window).mean()
    std = close.rolling(window).std()
    upper = middle + (num_std * std)
    lower = middle - (num_std * std)
    
    signals = pd.Series(0, index=close.index)
    signals[close < lower] = 1   # Long when below lower band
    signals[close > upper] = -1  # Short when above upper band
    signals[close.between(middle - std, middle + std)] = 0  # Exit near middle
    
    return signals
props.explanation: The bands are a z-score in price units, so this is the [[Z-Score]] rule with a moving standard deviation: two deviations out, and back to the mean. It fails exactly where [[Mean Reversion]] fails -- when the band is being walked rather than tested.

atoms.title: rsi mean reversion
atoms.summary: Buys oversold and sells overbought on RSI, exiting as it returns to the midpoint.

props.formula:
def rsi_mean_reversion(rsi, oversold=30, overbought=70, exit=50):
    signals = pd.Series(0, index=rsi.index)
    signals[rsi < oversold] = 1   # Long when oversold
    signals[rsi > overbought] = -1  # Short when overbought
    
    # Exit conditions
    # Long exit: RSI crosses above exit threshold
    # Short exit: RSI crosses below exit threshold
    
    return signals
props.explanation: The same trade as the band version with a bounded oscillator in place of a distance: thirty and seventy rather than two deviations, and fifty as the exit. Chapter 6 states the caution that matters here -- in a strong trend RSI shifts its range and stays extreme.

atoms.title: mean-reversion half-life
atoms.summary: Time for deviation to decay by half.

props.formula:
def calculate_half_life(spread):
    spread_lag = spread.shift(1)
    spread_diff = spread - spread_lag
    
    # Regress: spread_diff = beta * spread_lag + error
    spread_lag = spread_lag.dropna()
    spread_diff = spread_diff.dropna()
    
    model = OLS(spread_diff, spread_lag).fit()
    half_life = -np.log(2) / model.params[0]
    
    return half_life
props.explanation: Half-life < 5 days: Fast mean reversion, good for short-term trading Half-life 5-30 days: Moderate, suitable for swing trading Half-life > 30 days: Slow, may be trending or structural

atoms.title: donchian channel breakout
atoms.summary: Breakout of N-period high or low.

props.formula:
Upper Channel = Highest High over N periods
Lower Channel = Lowest Low over N periods
def donchian_breakout(high, low, close, entry_period=20, exit_period=10):
    upper = high.rolling(entry_period).max()
    lower = low.rolling(entry_period).min()
    
    exit_upper = high.rolling(exit_period).max()
    exit_lower = low.rolling(exit_period).min()
    
    signals = pd.Series(0, index=close.index)
    signals[close > upper.shift(1)] = 1   # Long breakout
    signals[close < lower.shift(1)] = -1  # Short breakout
    
    # Exit signals
    exit_long = close < exit_lower.shift(1)
    exit_short = close > exit_upper.shift(1)
    
    return signals, exit_long, exit_short
props.explanation: Entry: 20-period (Turtle system) Exit: 10-period Variations: 55-period for longer-term

def bollinger_squeeze(close, bb_period=20, keltner_period=20, bb_std=2, kelt_mult=1.5):
    # Bollinger Bands
    bb_middle = close.rolling(bb_period).mean()
    bb_std_val = close.rolling(bb_period).std()
    bb_upper = bb_middle + bb_std * bb_std_val
    bb_lower = bb_middle - bb_std * bb_std_val
    
    # Keltner Channels (for squeeze detection)
    # ATR calculation needed
    # ...
    
    # Squeeze: BB inside Keltner
    squeeze = (bb_upper < kelt_upper) & (bb_lower > kelt_lower)
    
    # Breakout: Price closes outside BB after squeeze
    breakout_up = (close > bb_upper) & squeeze.shift(1)
    breakout_down = (close < bb_lower) & squeeze.shift(1)
    
    return squeeze, breakout_up, breakout_down

atoms.title: breakout confirmation filters
atoms.summary: Requires volume above its average, or momentum in the breakout direction, before a break counts.

props.formula:
def volume_confirmed_breakout(price_breakout, volume, avg_volume_period=20, threshold=1.5):
    avg_volume = volume.rolling(avg_volume_period).mean()
    volume_confirmation = volume > (threshold * avg_volume)
    
    confirmed_breakout = price_breakout & volume_confirmation
    return confirmed_breakout
def momentum_confirmed_breakout(price_breakout, rsi, rsi_threshold=50):
    # Bullish breakout confirmed by RSI > 50
    # Bearish breakout confirmed by RSI < 50
    bullish_confirmed = price_breakout & (price_breakout > 0) & (rsi > rsi_threshold)
    bearish_confirmed = price_breakout & (price_breakout < 0) & (rsi < rsi_threshold)
    
    return bullish_confirmed, bearish_confirmed
props.explanation: The chapter puts breakout failure at fifty to sixty per cent, and both filters attack the same failure: a level given up without participation behind it. The cost is the breaks that run without waiting.
